analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop excipient-free molnupiravir microparticles for pulmonary drug delivery and evaluate their properties using machine learning. The background highlights molnupiravir's broad-spectrum antiviral activity against various viruses, including Ebola virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved preparing molnupiravir microparticles using spray freeze-drying and jet milling methods. The microparticles were analyzed for their structural and aerodynamic properties, with the optimal inhalable powder being tested for performance metrics.
analysis.methods: Molnupiravir microparticles were prepared by spray freeze-drying and jet milling. Machine learning was employed to assess the impact of process parameters like feeding rate, concentration, and nebulization pressure on the resulting powder characteristics.
analysis.main_results: SEM images revealed that microparticles produced by spray freeze-drying had a porous and near-spherical structure. The fine particle fraction and mass median aerodynamic diameter of the optimal inhalable powder reached 70.19 ± 2.06% and 2.80 ± 0.16 μm, respectively, indicating good aerodynamic performance.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The results suggest that the developed microparticles have favorable structural and aerodynamic properties for pulmonary drug delivery. This approach offers a novel method for formulating antiviral drugs for targeted respiratory administration.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of more effective pulmonary drug delivery systems for antiviral therapies, potentially improving treatment outcomes for respiratory viral infections, including Ebola virus disease.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to short-term storage behavior and does not provide long-term stability data. The evidence is moderate as it is based on abstract-only information and does not include detailed clinical or epidemiological outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study focuses on the preparation of excipient-free molnupiravir microparticles for pulmonary drug delivery and evaluates their properties using machine learning. The background highlights molnupiravir's broad-spectrum antiviral activity, including against Ebola virus. The methods involved spray freeze-drying and jet milling to create microparticles, with machine learning used to analyze the effects of process parameters on powder properties. Results showed that the microparticles had a porous and near-spherical structure, with excellent aerodynamic performance, as evidenced by a fine particle fraction of 70.19 ± 2.06% and a mass median aerodynamic diameter of 2.80 ± 0.16 μm. The authors concluded that the microparticles demonstrated preliminary short-term storage stability, suggesting a novel approach for formulating antiviral drugs for respiratory administration. The findings may contribute to the development of more effective pulmonary delivery systems for antiviral therapies, particularly for diseases like Ebola virus disease. However, the study is limited to short-term storage behavior and abstract-only data, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

papers.title_zh: 用于肺部药物输送的无赋形剂莫努匹拉韦微粒的制备和通过机器学习的过程评估
papers.source_body_en: Background/Objective: Molnupiravir (EIDD-2801) was originally designed to treat influenza A virus and showed broad-spectrum antiviral activity, including against influenza virus, Ebola virus, coronavirus and other viruses. Methods: In this study, molnupiravir microparticles were firstly prepared by spray freeze-drying (SFD) and jet milling (JM) methods. Meanwhile, machine learning methodology was applied to evaluate the influence of process parameters such as feeding rate, concentration, and nebulization pressure on powder properties. Results: According to SEM images, the microparticles prepared by SFD presented a porous and near-spherical structure. Moreover, the fine particle fraction (FPF) and mass median aerodynamic diameter (MMAD) of the optimal inhalable powder reached up to 70.19 ± 2.06% and 2.80 ± 0.16 μm, proving the excellent aerodynamic performance. Conclusions: The molnupiravir micropowder showed preliminary short-term storage behavior after storage for 28 days at 25 °C and 60% RH.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景/目的:Molnupiravir (EIDD-2801)最初设计用于治疗甲型流感病毒,并表现出广谱抗病毒药物活性,包括对抗流感病毒、埃博拉病毒、冠状病毒和其他病毒。方法:本研究首先采用喷雾冷冻干燥(SFD)和气流粉碎(JM)方法制备莫努匹拉韦微粒。同时,应用机器学习方法评估加料速率、浓度和雾化压力等工艺参数对粉末性能的影响。结果:从SEM图像来看,SFD制备的微粒呈现出多孔且近球形的结构。此外,最佳可吸入粉末的细颗粒分数(FPF)和质量中值空气动力学直径(MMAD)分别达到70.19±2.06%和2.80±0.16μm,证明了其优异的空气动力学性能。结论:莫努匹拉韦微粉在25°C、60%RH条件下储存28天后表现出初步的短期储存行为。

papers.title: Improving the Resolution and Informativity of the Majority-Rule Consensus Tree Using Fine-Grained Dissimilarity Measures
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic analyses often require the summarization of multiple trees, e.g., in Bayesian analyses to obtain the centroid of the posterior distribution of trees, or to determine the consensus of a set of bootstrap trees. The majority-rule consensus tree is the most commonly used. It is easy to compute and minimizes the sum of Robinson-Foulds (RF) distances to the input trees. In mathematical terms, the majority-rule consensus tree is the median of the input trees with respect to the RF distance. However, due to the coarse nature of RF distance, which only considers whether two branches induce exactly the same bipartition of the taxa or not, highly unresolved trees can be produced when the phylogenetic signal is low. To overcome this limitation, we propose using median trees with respect to finer-grained dissimilarity measures between trees. These measures include a quartet distance between tree topologies, and transfer distances, which quantify the similarity between bipartitions, in contrast to the presence/absence view of RF. We describe fast heuristic consensus algorithms for transfer-based tree dissimilarities, capable of efficiently processing trees with thousands of taxa. Through evaluations on simulated datasets in both Bayesian and bootstrapping maximum-likelihood frameworks, our results show that our methods improve consensus tree resolution in scenarios with low to moderate phylogenetic signal, while providing better or comparable dissimilarities to the true phylogeny. Applying our methods to mammals, Ebola virus, and a large HIV dataset of over nine thousand taxa confirms the improvement with real data. These results demonstrate the usefulness of our new consensus tree methods for analyzing the large datasets that are available today. Our software, PhyloCRISP, is available from https://github.com/yukiregista/PhyloCRISP.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a new method for improving the resolution and informativity of consensus trees in phylogenetic analyses by using fine-grained dissimilarity measures instead of the traditional Robinson-Foulds (RF) distance. The majority-rule consensus tree, commonly used in Bayesian and bootstrapping analyses, is known to produce highly unresolved trees when phylogenetic signal is low. The proposed method employs quartet distances and transfer distances to better capture the similarity between bipartitions. Evaluations on simulated datasets and real-world data, including Ebola virus and HIV datasets, demonstrate that the new approach enhances consensus tree resolution in low to moderate signal scenarios. The study highlights the importance of these methods for analyzing large datasets, particularly those involving human-pathogenic orthoebolaviruses, and suggests their potential utility in understanding viral evolution and improving outbreak response. The evidence is based on computational performance and is considered moderate in strength due to the absence of direct clinical or epidemiological outcomes.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 系统发育分析通常需要对多个树进行汇总,例如,在贝叶斯分析中以获得树后验分布的质心,或确定一组引导树的共识。多数规则共识树是最常用的。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究描述了一种使用细粒度相异性度量来提高共识树分辨率的计算方法。它在模拟数据集和现实世界数据(包括哺乳动物、埃博拉病毒 和包含 9000 多个分类群的大型 HIV 数据集)上评估该方法。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法涉及针对基于转移的树差异开发快速启发式共识算法,该算法量化二分之间的相似性,而不是使用粗略的 Robinson-Foulds (RF) 距离。这些算法旨在有效地处理具有数千个分类单元的树。
elements_zh.main_results: 通过对贝叶斯和自举最大似然框架中的模拟数据集进行评估,结果表明,所提出的方法在具有低至中等系统发育信号的情况下提高了共识树分辨率,同时提供了与真实 系统发育 更好或相当的差异。将这些方法应用于实际数据证实了这种改进。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,他们的新共识树方法信息更丰富,更适合分析具有低至中等系统发育信号的大型数据集。新颖之处在于使用细粒度的相异性度量来捕获二分之间更详细的关系。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以通过提供更准确和更清晰的共识树,为大型系统发育数据集的分析提供信息,特别是那些涉及人类致病性正埃博拉病毒的数据集。这对于理解病毒 进化 和改善 暴发 反应具有重要意义。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于模拟和真实数据集,方法的有效性可能取决于输入数据的质量和数量。证据强度中等,因为结果是基于计算评估而不是临床或流行病学结果。

analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the analysis of large phylogenetic datasets, particularly those involving human-pathogenic orthoebolaviruses, by providing more accurate and resolved consensus trees. This has implications for understanding viral evolution and improving outbreak response.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to simulated and real datasets, and the effectiveness of the methods may depend on the quality and quantity of the input data. The evidence strength is moderate, as the results are based on computational evaluations rather than clinical or epidemiological outcomes.

papers.title_zh: 使用细粒度相异性度量提高多数规则共识树的分辨率和信息量
papers.source_body_en: Phylogenetic analyses often require the summarization of multiple trees, e.g., in Bayesian analyses to obtain the centroid of the posterior distribution of trees, or to determine the consensus of a set of bootstrap trees. The majority-rule consensus tree is the most commonly used. It is easy to compute and minimizes the sum of Robinson-Foulds (RF) distances to the input trees. In mathematical terms, the majority-rule consensus tree is the median of the input trees with respect to the RF distance. However, due to the coarse nature of RF distance, which only considers whether two branches induce exactly the same bipartition of the taxa or not, highly unresolved trees can be produced when the phylogenetic signal is low. To overcome this limitation, we propose using median trees with respect to finer-grained dissimilarity measures between trees. These measures include a quartet distance between tree topologies, and transfer distances, which quantify the similarity between bipartitions, in contrast to the presence/absence view of RF. We describe fast heuristic consensus algorithms for transfer-based tree dissimilarities, capable of efficiently processing trees with thousands of taxa. Through evaluations on simulated datasets in both Bayesian and bootstrapping maximum-likelihood frameworks, our results show that our methods improve consensus tree resolution in scenarios with low to moderate phylogenetic signal, while providing better or comparable dissimilarities to the true phylogeny. Applying our methods to mammals, Ebola virus, and a large HIV dataset of over nine thousand taxa confirms the improvement with real data. These results demonstrate the usefulness of our new consensus tree methods for analyzing the large datasets that are available today. Our software, PhyloCRISP, is available from https://github.com/yukiregista/PhyloCRISP.
papers.abstract_zh: 系统发育分析通常需要对多个树进行汇总,例如,在贝叶斯分析中以获得树后验分布的质心,或确定一组引导树的共识。多数规则共识树是最常用的。它很容易计算并最小化到输入树的 Robinson-Foulds (RF) 距离之和。用数学术语来说,多数规则共识树是输入树相对于 RF 距离的中值。然而,由于RF距离的粗略性质,仅考虑两个分支是否引起完全相同的类群二分,当系统发育信号较低时,可能会产生高度未解析的树。为了克服这一限制,我们建议使用中值树来实现树之间更细粒度的相异性度量。这些度量包括树拓扑之间的四重距离和传输距离,它们量化了二分区之间的相似性,与 RF 的存在/不存在视图形成对比。我们描述了基于转移的树差异的快速启发式共识算法,能够有效地处理具有数千个类群的树。通过对贝叶斯和引导最大似然框架中的模拟数据集进行评估,我们的结果表明,我们的方法在具有低到中等系统发育信号的情况下提高了共识树分辨率,同时提供了与真实 系统发育 更好或相当的差异。将我们的方法应用于哺乳动物、埃博拉病毒 和超过 9000 个分类单元的大型 HIV 数据集,证实了真实数据的改进。这些结果证明了我们新的共识树方法在分析当今可用的大型数据集方面的有用性。我们的软件 PhyloCRISP 可从 https://github.com/yukiregista/PhyloCRISP 获取。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 系统发育分析通常需要对多个树进行汇总,例如,在贝叶斯分析中以获得树后验分布的质心,或确定一组引导树的共识。多数规则共识树是最常用的。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究描述了一种使用细粒度相异性度量来提高共识树分辨率的计算方法。它在模拟数据集和现实世界数据(包括哺乳动物、埃博拉病毒 和包含 9000 多个分类群的大型 HIV 数据集)上评估该方法。
analysis_zh.methods: 这些方法涉及针对基于转移的树差异开发快速启发式共识算法,该算法量化二分之间的相似性,而不是使用粗略的 Robinson-Foulds (RF) 距离。这些算法旨在有效地处理具有数千个分类单元的树。
analysis_zh.main_results: 通过对贝叶斯和自举最大似然框架中的模拟数据集进行评估,结果表明,所提出的方法在具有低至中等系统发育信号的情况下提高了共识树分辨率,同时提供了与真实 系统发育 更好或相当的差异。将这些方法应用于实际数据证实了这种改进。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,他们的新共识树方法信息更丰富,更适合分析具有低至中等系统发育信号的大型数据集。新颖之处在于使用细粒度的相异性度量来捕获二分之间更详细的关系。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以通过提供更准确和更清晰的共识树,为大型系统发育数据集的分析提供信息,特别是那些涉及人类致病性正埃博拉病毒的数据集。这对于理解病毒 进化 和改善 暴发 反应具有重要意义。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于模拟和真实数据集,方法的有效性可能取决于输入数据的质量和数量。证据强度中等,因为结果是基于计算评估而不是临床或流行病学结果。

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 3 more Ebola Outbreak, DRC and Region, Situation Report #14 (October 13, 2026) Format Situation Report Source IMC Posted 13 Oct 2026 Originally published 13 Oct 2026 Attachments Download Report (PDF | 306.01 KB) FAST FACTS On May 15, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak of Ebola virus disease (EVD), later confirmed to be caused by the Bundibugyo strain. As of October 11, 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 confirmed deaths had been reported in the DRC. On October 5, a case of imported EVD was confirmed in Kenya. The patient had traveled from the DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he died. No EVD cases have been confirmed in South Sudan or the Central African Republic, but risk of cross-border transmission remains high due to transient populations and porous borders with the DRC. In the DRC, the outbreak remains centered in Ituri province, but cases have also been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi and Tshopo provinces, indicating an uncontrolled spread of the disease. Uganda has officially declared its outbreak to be over, though preparedness activities continue. OUR RESPONSE Across the region, our teams are providing case management, infection prevention and control, screening and triage, risk communication and community engagement, training and preparedness planning. We are helping more than 110 facilities screen, identify and treat EVD. Our supported sites in the DRC have conducted more than 1 million EVD screenings and provided treatment to 2,806 patients, including 828 confirmed cases. We have so far trained 6,451 people in the DRC on EVD case management, response and transmission prevention. With the support of the US Department of State, DG ECHO and other donors, International Medical Corps teams in the DRC, South Sudan and Uganda are actively responding to the outbreak and collaborating closely with ministries of health, key actors and response partners. International Medical Corps has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared to provide case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthen IPC in referring health facilities, conduct screening and triage, support risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) in surrounding communities and train health workers on EVD response protocols. International Medical Corps has used a hub-and-spoke model since the outbreak was declared to provide case-management support at designated treatment and transit facilities, strengthen IPC in referring health facilities, conduct screening and triage, support risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) in surrounding communities and train health workers on EVD response protocols. news.source_body_en: This report details the ongoing Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), declared on May 15, 2026, and confirmed to be caused by the Bundibugyo strain. As of October 11, 2026, 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 confirmed deaths have been reported, with the outbreak spreading to multiple provinces including Ituri, Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi, and Tshopo. An imported case was confirmed in Kenya on October 5, 2026, involving a patient who traveled from the DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he died. The risk of cross-border transmission remains high in South Sudan and the Central African Republic due to porous borders and transient populations. International Medical Corps teams are actively responding in the DRC, South Sudan, and Uganda, providing case management, infection prevention and control, screening, and training. Uganda has officially declared its outbreak over, though preparedness activities continue. The response includes a hub-and-spoke model to support treatment facilities and strengthen infection control measures.

Log out Home Donate Sponsor a Child Gift Catalog About Us Our Work Ways to Help News & Stories Partnerships Churches Schools Corporations From the Field 2026 Ebola virus outbreak: Facts, FAQs, and how to help Photo A health worker carries medication to a confirmed Ebola patient at an Ebola treatment center near Butembo in North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, as part of the ongoing response to the outbreak. (© 2026 World Vision/photo by Christelle Lasha) EmailFacebookPinterestTwitterShare Ebola remains a serious global health threat, with an outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease, a strain of Ebola, continuing in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and a case now confirmed in Kenya. In May 2026, DRC declared an Ebola outbreak in Ituri province involving a newly identified variant that had not matched previously known strains. With no vaccine currently available for this variant, thousands of displaced children are at risk. The World Health Organization (WHO) continues to classify the 2026 Ebola outbreak as a public health emergency of international concern. On Oct. 6, 2026, Kenya confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease. The patient, who had traveled from DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, Kenya, died after being hospitalized and isolated. Kenya’s Ministry of Health is tracing and monitoring people who may have been exposed and has emphasized that Kenya does not currently have an Ebola outbreak. The developments in DRC and Kenya highlight the importance of early detection, contact tracing, infection prevention and accurate information in limiting the spread of Ebola. The outbreak is unfolding in communities already facing insecurity, displacement, food insecurity and limited access to health care, conditions that can make it harder to identify cases quickly and provide timely care. For children and families living in affected communities, Ebola can bring additional fear, disruption, and loss. World Vision is working with health authorities and communities to promote prevention, strengthen preparedness, support vulnerable children and families, and help counter misinformation. Ebola virus disease: Facts, FAQs, and how to help Fast facts: Ebola What is Ebola? What is happening with the Ebola outbreak in DRC? Has Ebola been reported in Kenya? What are the symptoms of Ebola? Is Ebola treatable? How does World Vision respond to Ebola outbreaks? What was World Vision’s response to the Ebola outbreaks in 2014? How can I help Ebola survivors and people affected by viruses? Fast facts: Ebola virus disease Ebolavirus is highly contagious and can cause Ebola virus disease (EVD), formerly known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever. The disease is initially transmitted to humans from wild animals. Subsequently, it spreads by human-to-human transmission through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected people. It can also be transmitted through contact with surfaces contaminated with these fluids. In 1976, public health officials identified ebolaviruses during two successive outbreaks of lethal hemorrhagic fever in distinct regions of Central Africa. The initial outbreak occurred in a village near the Ebola River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), giving the virus its name. The second outbreak occurred an estimated 500 miles away in what is now South Sudan. Ebola outbreaks primarily occur in Central and West Africa, with occasional cases in other regions. Recent outbreaks have been confirmed in DRC (2018–2020), Uganda (2022–2023), and DRC’s Kasai and Ituri provinces (2026). In October 2026, Kenya confirmed its first imported case of an Ebola strain, Bundibugyo virus disease, linked to the ongoing outbreak in DRC. CDC officials say the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is very low. BACK TO QUESTIONS You can deliver hope and help amid emergencies. Give Now What is Ebola? Ebola virus disease, formerly known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever, is a rare and often deadly disease in humans caused by infection with one of four ebolavirus strains: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, or Taï Forest. BACK TO QUESTIONS To date, Ebola disease cases linked to the outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo have been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi and Tshopo provinces. Cases linked to the DRC outbreak have also been reported in Kampala, Uganda, and one case has been reported in Kenya. (Graphic courtesy of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) What is happening with the Ebola outbreak in DRC? On May 15, 2026, DRC officials declared a new Ebola outbreak in the health zones of Bunia, Mongwalu, and Rwampara in Ituri Province. Since then, the virus has spread rapidly, becoming the world’s second-largest Ebola epidemic on record, according to government data, as transmission continues to outpace efforts to contain it. The outbreak is especially concerning because it is occurring amid insecurity, population displacement, high population movement, and limited access to health services in some affected communities. These conditions can make it harder for health workers and humanitarian organizations to identify cases quickly, trace contacts, and provide timely care. As of Oct. 4, 2026: 8,625 confirmed cases have been reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 4,151 confirmed deaths have been recorded. The outbreak was affecting 62 health zones across seven provinces. Ituri remained the main center of transmission, although cases have continued to increase in other provinces. The situation remains fluid, and case numbers can change as authorities identify, test, and report additional cases. The WHO continues to classify the outbreak as a public health emergency of international concern. World Vision is also working alongside health authorities and humanitarian partners to help contain the 17th outbreak and protect vulnerable children and families through hygiene promotion, infection prevention and control, child protection support, community education, and coordination with local leaders. BACK TO QUESTIONS During community activities in North Kivu, World Vision staff reinforced Ebola prevention measures by providing handwashing stations, promoting hand hygiene, and encouraging physical distancing. Community members also received information on recognizing Ebola symptoms and accessing health services, helping reduce the risk of transmission while supporting affected families. (© 2026 World Vision/photo by Christelle Lasha) Has Ebola been reported in Kenya? Yes. On October 6, 2026, Kenya’s Ministry of Health confirmed the country’s first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease, a strain of Ebola. The patient, a Kenyan citizen who had traveled from DRC through Uganda, arrived in Nairobi on Oct. 3. After developing symptoms, the patient was isolated and received medical care but died Oct. 5. A safe and dignified burial was conducted in accordance with Ebola prevention protocols. Kenya’s Ministry of Health has emphasized that this is an imported case and that Kenya does not currently have an Ebola outbreak. Health authorities are tracing and monitoring people who may have been exposed to prevent further transmission. BACK TO QUESTIONS What are the symptoms of Ebola? Symptoms of Ebola virus disease include high body temperature, headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and both internal and external bleeding, such as from the gums and stool. It can be challenging to distinguish Ebola from other diseases, such as malaria, typhoid fever, and meningitis. Symptoms typically appear from 2 to 21 days after contracting the disease. People who have contracted the disease can’t transmit it to others until symptoms appear. BACK TO QUESTIONS In response to the 2025 Ebola outbreak, World Vision launched a targeted vaccination campaign to help protect humanitarian staff working in affected areas. In partnership with Congolese health authorities, the World Health Organization, and the Expanded Programme on Immunization, the effort supported WHO-recommended ring vaccination strategies. Plans were designed to help contain the spread of the virus and protect frontline workers and communities at the highest risk. (© 2026 World Vision) BACK TO QUESTIONS Is Ebola treatable? While there is no proven, licensed treatment for Ebola, early symptom management and intravenous fluid hydration can improve survival rates. Ongoing research efforts are exploring potential treatments, including antiviral drugs and immunotherapies. The 2026 Ituri outbreak is especially concerning because the newly identified variant currently has no vaccine available. (© 2025 World Vision/photo by Jean-Baptiste Mirindi) How does World Vision respond to Ebola outbreaks? World Vision responds swiftly to Ebola outbreaks by educating affected communities, supporting healthcare workers, providing child protection and psychosocial support, ensuring access to clean water and sanitation, and delivering emergency relief. We aim to help communities stay safe and resilient in the face of this deadly virus. A few of our key programming areas include: Community education: We equip communities with information about Ebola prevention, transmission, and the importance of early detection. We help raise awareness to ensure people know how to protect themselves from the virus. World Vision’s Channels of Hope programming: We train and equip religious leaders to share accurate information about Ebola prevention and treatment, dispel myths and misconceptions, and promote safe practices within their congregations and communities. By working with these local faith leaders, who have a great deal of influence because of how much their communities trust them, World Vision seeks to enhance awareness, reduce stigmatization, and encourage early detection and treatment of Ebola cases. The collaborative approach between faith-based organizations, communities, and health agencies has played a vital role in controlling the spread of Ebola and providing support to affected individuals and families. Child protection: We offer psychosocial support to children who may have lost family members or been affected by the outbreak. We work to keep children safe and emotionally supported. Healthcare support: We supply healthcare workers with medical supplies, protective gear, and training so they can safely care for Ebola patients. World Vision swiftly responded to the 2014 Ebola virus outbreak in Sierra Leone. We did this through a comprehensive effort to protect children and their families. With a strong focus on health and safety, awareness and prevention, safe burials, and social and economic recovery, World Vision played a crucial role in combating the epidemic. Our initiatives ranged from providing personal protective equipment and hygiene kits to launching extensive education campaigns and training local leaders on virus prevention. Through our efforts, we successfully prevented Ebola-related deaths among the children and families we supported. And we contributed significantly to the containment of the outbreak. Our approach encompassed immediate medical needs, long-term recovery, and community resilience. When Ebola struck Sierra Leone in 2014, World Vision was already working in 25 program areas. We were serving an estimated 58,000 children and their families. Building on 20 years of community development in Sierra Leone, we joined communities, partner agencies, and every level of government in the battle against Ebola. In fact, they have often been shunned, ostracized, vilified because they are burial workers.” BACK TO QUESTIONS To prevent the spread of Ebola during the 2019 outbreak in the DRC, teacher Françoise Mbambu teaches a student how to wash his hands. Pray for families who have lost loved ones, people who are sick or under quarantine, and the health workers caring for them. Pray also for the organizations working to contain the virus, and for the children and families across the region. Subsequently, it spreads by human-to-human transmission through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected people. It can also be transmitted through contact with surfaces contaminated with these fluids. In 1976, public health officials identified ebolaviruses during two successive outbreaks of lethal hemorrhagic fever in distinct regions of Central Africa. Recent outbreaks have been confirmed in DRC (2018–2020), Uganda (2022–2023), and DRC’s Kasai and Ituri provinces (2026). In October 2026, Kenya confirmed its first imported case of an Ebola strain, Bundibugyo virus disease, linked to the ongoing outbreak in DRC. CDC officials say the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is very low. BACK TO QUESTIONS You can deliver hope and help amid emergencies. Give Now What is Ebola? analysis_en.time: The 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) was declared on May 15, 2026, and by October 6, 2026, the situation had escalated. Kenya confirmed its first imported case on October 6, 2026, and the patient died after hospitalization and isolation.
analysis_en.location_and_population: The outbreak is primarily in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), specifically in Ituri Province, affecting communities in Bunia, Mongwalu, and Rwampara. It has also spread to other provinces in DRC and to Kampala, Uganda, and Kenya. The affected population includes thousands of displaced children and vulnerable communities.
analysis_en.event: An Ebola outbreak involving a newly identified variant of the Bundibugyo virus was declared in Ituri Province, DRC, on May 15, 2026. Kenya confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease on October 6, 2026, which was linked to the ongoing DRC outbreak. The patient died after being hospitalized and isolated.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: As of October 6, 2026, 8,625 confirmed cases and 4,151 confirmed deaths have been reported in the DRC. The outbreak is the world’s second-largest on record. Thousands of displaced children are at risk due to the lack of a vaccine for this variant. Kenya’s Ministry of Health is tracing and monitoring people who may have been exposed, but it has emphasized that Kenya does not currently have an outbreak.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The World Health Organization (WHO) continues to classify the 2026 outbreak as a public health emergency of international concern. Kenya’s Ministry of Health is conducting contact tracing and monitoring. World Vision is working with health authorities to promote prevention, strengthen preparedness, and support vulnerable children and families. The CDC states the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is very low.

news.source_body_en: In 2026, an Ebola outbreak involving a newly identified variant of the Bundibugyo virus was declared in Ituri Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), on May 15. By October 6, the outbreak had become the world’s second-largest, with 8,625 confirmed cases and 4,151 deaths. The DRC outbreak is occurring in communities facing insecurity, displacement, and limited healthcare access, complicating containment efforts. On October 6, Kenya confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease, linked to the DRC outbreak, which resulted in the patient’s death after hospitalization and isolation. Kenya’s Ministry of Health is tracing contacts but has stated there is no current outbreak. The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies the situation as a public health emergency of international concern. World Vision is collaborating with health authorities to support prevention, preparedness, and vulnerable communities. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is very low. The outbreak highlights the need for early detection, accurate information, and effective response measures to limit its spread.

A team of researchers from Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Belgium, France, the United States and beyond has now provided the first systematic computational assessment of that question, and their findings are a mixture of reassurance and caution. Writing in Nature Communications, the group reports that while one leading antibody cocktail appears to retain its targeting of the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein, another widely deployed therapeutic may be compromised by mutations at its binding site, underscoring how quickly genomic surveillance must be coupled to therapeutic decision-making during an active outbreak. The study, led by Kevin Cissy Nabukeera, Gradi Luakanda-Ndelemo and Syrus Semawule, with joint supervision from Daudi Jjingo, Tony Wawina-Bokalanga, Placide Mbala-Kingebeni and Isaac Ssewanyana, drew on 44 Bundibugyo virus genome sequences, including 12 generated from the ongoing 2026 outbreak. The team’s central analytical target was the viral glycoprotein, the trimeric surface spike that mediates attachment and entry into host cells and that serves as the sole target of the current generation of approved and investigational ebolavirus antibody therapeutics. Because these antibodies were raised and clinically evaluated against Ebola virus, the Zaire ebolavirus species, their cross-reactivity with Bundibugyo virus cannot be assumed, and the researchers set out to map precisely where the two viruses’ glycoproteins agree and diverge at the amino acid level. The analytical strategy combined genomic comparison with structural modelling. By aligning the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein sequences against the Ebola virus reference and projecting the resulting substitutions onto three-dimensional models of the glycoprotein trimer, the team could identify which residues fall within the epitopes, the antibody-binding footprints, of the major therapeutic candidates. Where substitutions occurred within or adjacent to these footprints, the researchers used structural prediction tools, including resources from Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold suite, to model how the altered residues would affect the geometry, charge complementarity and binding affinity of the antibody-antigen interface. This approach allowed the team to generate predictions of therapeutic efficacy rapidly, without waiting for the slow process of isolating and testing live virus in high-containment laboratories. The most concerning finding concerns mAb114, marketed as Ebanga, a monoclonal antibody that received regulatory approval for the treatment of Ebola virus disease following its demonstration of survival benefit in the PALM trial conducted during the 2018-2020 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The computational analysis revealed that two mutations in the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein, E112D and P116A, fall within the mAb114 epitope. According to the structural models, these substitutions do not merely weaken binding; they cause the antibody to engage in off-target binding and substantially reduce its affinity for the viral surface. In practical terms, the models predict that mAb114’s efficacy against Bundibugyo virus may be compromised, a result that, if confirmed experimentally, would have immediate implications for treatment protocols in the affected region. The picture for the second major therapeutic, the three-antibody cocktail known as Inmazeb, proved more complex and, in some respects, more encouraging. Inmazeb combines atoltivimab, maftivimab and odesivimab, three antibodies that bind distinct sites on the Ebola virus glycoprotein and were also validated in the PALM trial. The structural modelling showed that odesivimab maintains its epitope binding against the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein, but that atoltivimab and maftivimab individually fail to bind their designated sites on the Bundibugyo virus spike. Crucially, however, when the complete trimeric cocktail was modelled against the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein, the analysis demonstrated synergistic binding, suggesting that the cooperative action of the three antibodies together may preserve therapeutic activity even where individual components fall short. This combinatorial effect carries a broader lesson for antiviral therapeutics. Antibody cocktails were originally designed with viral escape in mind: targeting multiple non-overlapping epitopes makes it far harder for a virus to mutate its way around the treatment. The Bundibugyo virus analysis adds a second rationale, showing that cooperation between antibodies can compensate for the loss of individual binding interactions when a therapeutic is deployed against a related but antigenically divergent virus species. The authors emphasize that the complex binding behaviour of the Inmazeb components points to the importance of antibody combinatorial effects for treatment efficacy, a consideration that should inform both the design of future pan-ebolavirus therapeutics and the interpretation of cross-species efficacy predictions. By contrast, the analysis of the MBP134 cocktail offers the clearest cause for optimism. MBP134, a two-antibody combination developed to provide broad protection across ebolavirus species, was found to have epitopes that remain conserved in the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein. The computational models predict that MBP134 retains its conserved targeting and holds promise as a broadly protective therapeutic against the 2026 outbreak strain. Because MBP134 was explicitly engineered to bind conserved regions of the glycoprotein across the Orthoebolavirus genus, its resilience in this analysis is consistent with its design intent, and the finding positions it as a leading candidate for experimental deployment should clinical evaluation proceed. The authors are careful to frame their conclusions as predictions rather than proven clinical facts. Computational structural modelling, however sophisticated, cannot fully capture the dynamics of antibody-antigen interaction in biological systems, and neutralization assays performed with authentic Bundibugyo virus isolates remain the definitive test of therapeutic efficacy. The team explicitly calls for urgent experimental validation through neutralization assays, work that would require high-containment laboratory capacity and access to outbreak-derived viral stocks. The gap between computational prediction and wet-laboratory confirmation is a recurring challenge in outbreak response, and this study illustrates both the value and the limitations of moving fast with in silico evidence while definitive experiments are organized. The collaborative structure of the research reflects the realities of modern outbreak science. The analysis brought together the African Center of Excellence in Bioinformatics and Data-Intensive Sciences at Makerere University, the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale in Kinshasa, Uganda’s National Health Laboratory and Diagnostic Services, the Uganda Virus Research Institute, and partners including the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp, Université de Montpellier, the Pandemic Sciences Institute at Oxford, and several public health ministries and agencies across both affected countries. The work was supported in part by Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold tools and resources, a Google.org AIMaR grant, the US National Institutes of Health, the Gates Foundation and the Lacuna Fund, alongside the She Data Science programme supporting Ugandan women in health data science. This blend of African-led genomic capacity, international structural biology expertise and philanthropic and governmental funding represents a template for how future cross-border outbreak analyses can be assembled quickly. As the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak continues, the study’s practical message is twofold. First, treatment decisions in the field should not assume that Ebola virus therapeutics transfer automatically to Bundibugyo virus; the E112D and P116A substitutions that undermine mAb114 binding demonstrate that even single-residue changes at an epitope can reshape the therapeutic landscape. Second, genomic surveillance must be treated as a live input to therapeutic strategy, with continuous monitoring of glycoprotein sequences from new cases feeding into updated structural models and, ultimately, into neutralization testing. The rapid genomic and structural assessment published this week provides exactly that kind of early insight, and its predictions, once validated experimentally, could help determine which antibody therapies offer the best chance of saving lives in the current outbreak and in the Bundibugyo virus eruptions that will inevitably follow. The study, led by Kevin Cissy Nabukeera, Gradi Luakanda-Ndelemo and Syrus Semawule, with joint supervision from Daudi Jjingo, Tony Wawina-Bokalanga, Placide Mbala-Kingebeni and Isaac Ssewanyana, drew on 44 Bundibugyo virus genome sequences, including 12 generated from the ongoing 2026 outbreak. The team’s central analytical target was the viral glycoprotein, the trimeric surface spike that mediates attachment and entry into host cells and that serves as the sole target of the current generation of approved and investigational ebolavirus antibody therapeutics. Because these antibodies were raised and clinically evaluated against Ebola virus, the Zaire ebolavirus species, their cross-reactivity with Bundibugyo virus cannot be assumed, and the researchers set out to map precisely where the two viruses’ glycoproteins agree and diverge at the amino acid level. The analytical strategy combined genomic comparison with structural modelling. By aligning the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein sequences against the Ebola virus reference and projecting the resulting substitutions onto three-dimensional models of the glycoprotein trimer, the team could identify which residues fall within the epitopes, the antibody-binding footprints, of the major therapeutic candidates. Where substitutions occurred within or adjacent to these footprints, the researchers used structural prediction tools, including resources from Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold suite, to model how the altered residues would affect the geometry, charge complementarity and binding affinity of the antibody-antigen interface. This approach allowed the team to generate predictions of therapeutic efficacy rapidly, without waiting for the slow process of isolating and testing live virus in high-containment laboratories. The most concerning finding concerns mAb114, marketed as Ebanga, a monoclonal antibody that received regulatory approval for the treatment of Ebola virus disease following its demonstration of survival benefit in the PALM trial conducted during the 2018-2020 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The computational analysis revealed that two mutations in the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein, E112D and P116A, fall within the mAb114 epitope. According to the structural models, these substitutions do not merely weaken binding; they cause the antibody to engage in off-target binding and substantially reduce its affinity for the viral surface. In practical terms, the models predict that mAb114’s efficacy against Bundibugyo virus may be compromised, a result that, if confirmed experimentally, would have immediate implications for treatment protocols in the affected region. The picture for the second major therapeutic, the three-antibody cocktail known as Inmazeb, proved more complex and, in some respects, more encouraging. Inmazeb combines atoltivimab, maftivimab and odesivimab, three antibodies that bind distinct sites on the Ebola virus glycoprotein and were also validated in the PALM trial. The structural modelling showed that odesivimab maintains its epitope binding against the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein, but that atoltivimab and maftivimab individually fail to bind their designated sites on the Bundibugyo virus spike. Crucially, however, when the complete trimeric cocktail was modelled against the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein, the analysis demonstrated synergistic binding, suggesting that the cooperative action of the three antibodies together may preserve therapeutic activity even where individual components fall short. This combinatorial effect carries a broader lesson for antiviral therapeutics. Antibody cocktails were originally designed with viral escape in mind: targeting multiple non-overlapping epitopes makes it far harder for a virus to mutate its way around the treatment. The Bundibugyo virus analysis adds a second rationale, showing that cooperation between antibodies can compensate for the loss of individual binding interactions when a therapeutic is deployed against a related but antigenically divergent virus species. The authors emphasize that the complex binding behaviour of the Inmazeb components points to the importance of antibody combinatorial effects for treatment efficacy, a consideration that should inform both the design of future pan-ebolavirus therapeutics and the interpretation of cross-species efficacy predictions. By contrast, the analysis of the MBP134 cocktail offers the clearest cause for optimism. MBP134, a two-antibody combination developed to provide broad protection across ebolavirus species, was found to have epitopes that remain conserved in the Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein. The computational models predict that MBP134 retains its conserved targeting and holds promise as a broadly protective therapeutic against the 2026 outbreak strain. Because MBP134 was explicitly engineered to bind conserved regions of the glycoprotein across the Orthoebolavirus genus, its resilience in this analysis is consistent with its design intent, and the finding positions it as a leading candidate for experimental deployment should clinical evaluation proceed. The authors are careful to frame their conclusions as predictions rather than proven clinical facts. Computational structural modelling, however sophisticated, cannot fully capture the dynamics of antibody-antigen interaction in biological systems, and neutralization assays performed with authentic Bundibugyo virus isolates remain the definitive test of therapeutic efficacy. The team explicitly calls for urgent experimental validation through neutralization assays, work that would require high-containment laboratory capacity and access to outbreak-derived viral stocks. The gap between computational prediction and wet-laboratory confirmation is a recurring challenge in outbreak response, and this study illustrates both the value and the limitations of moving fast with in silico evidence while definitive experiments are organized. The collaborative structure of the research reflects the realities of modern outbreak science. The analysis brought together the African Center of Excellence in Bioinformatics and Data-Intensive Sciences at Makerere University, the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale in Kinshasa, Uganda’s National Health Laboratory and Diagnostic Services, the Uganda Virus Research Institute, and partners including the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp, Université de Montpellier, the Pandemic Sciences Institute at Oxford, and several public health ministries and agencies across both affected countries. The work was supported in part by Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold tools and resources, a Google.org AIMaR grant, the US National Institutes of Health, the Gates Foundation and the Lacuna Fund, alongside the She Data Science programme supporting Ugandan women in health data science. This blend of African-led genomic capacity, international structural biology expertise and philanthropic and governmental funding represents a template for how future cross-border outbreak analyses can be assembled quickly. As the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak continues, the study’s practical message is twofold. First, treatment decisions in the field should not assume that Ebola virus therapeutics transfer automatically to Bundibugyo virus; the E112D and P116A substitutions that undermine mAb114 binding demonstrate that even single-residue changes at an epitope can reshape the therapeutic landscape. Second, genomic surveillance must be treated as a live input to therapeutic strategy, with continuous monitoring of glycoprotein sequences from new cases feeding into updated structural models and, ultimately, into neutralization testing. The rapid genomic and structural assessment published this week provides exactly that kind of early insight, and its predictions, once validated experimentally, could help determine which antibody therapies offer the best chance of saving lives in the current outbreak and in the Bundibugyo virus eruptions that will inevitably follow. BODIES Govt Recognised In-House R&D Units AICTE Boards & Committees List of Indian CROs List of CROs (International) Govt & approved labs of India List of State Drugs Controllers Join Pharma | Login Home > News you can get e-magazine links on WhatsApp. Click here Clinical Trials + Font Resize - Uganda launches phase I clinical study of Bundibugyo virus disease vaccine Our Bureau, Mumbai Tuesday, October 13, 2026, 17:40 Hrs [IST] The Medical Research Council/Uganda Virus Research Institute and London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (MRC/UVRI & LSHTM Uganda Research Unit) has launched a phase I clinical study evaluating the safety and immunogenicity of a candidate vaccine against Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), a severe form of Ebola virus disease caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). The study is part of an international effort to develop vaccines against Ebola virus species for which no licensed vaccines are currently available. Conducted in partnership with the Oxford Vaccine Group and Pandemic Science Institute, at the University of Oxford, the study will evaluate the safety of a ChAdOx-based Bundibugyo Ebola vaccine candidate, ChAdOx BDBV, and its ability to stimulate an immune response in healthy adult volunteers. The ChAdOx BDBV vaccine candidate was developed by scientists at the University of Oxford, with production and quality-testing of the viral seed stock that formed the starting material for large-scale vaccine manufacture carried out onsite by the Clinical Biomanufacturing Facility. The Serum Institute of India (SII), based in Pune, India, has collaborated to manufacture and stockpiled approximately 620,000 doses of the ChAdOx1 BDBV vaccine candidate in two weeks for potential future use. SII has supplied 300 vials to UK and additionally ~3000 investigational doses for this phase I trial in Uganda. The Uganda study is led by Professor Eugene Ruzagira, Head of Clinical Research and Trials at the MRC/UVRI&LSHTM Uganda Research Unit, and will be conducted at the Unit's internationally recognized clinical research site in Masaka City, southwestern Uganda. With more than three decades of experience in vaccine research and clinical trials, the site combines state-of-the-art laboratory and clinical infrastructure, and long-standing community partnerships, providing an ideal setting for conducting early-phase clinical studies to the highest scientific, ethical and regulatory standards. CEPI, SII and the University of Oxford are committed to enabling rapid, affordable supply of Bundibugyo virus vaccines to affected countries and to the populations that need them. Bundibugyo virus was first identified during an outbreak in western Uganda in 2007 and remains one of the Ebola virus species for which no licenced vaccine is currently available. Developing an effective vaccine against Bundibugyo virus is therefore an important priority for global epidemic preparedness. The study further strengthens the MRC/UVRI& LSHTM Uganda Research Unit's longstanding contribution to research on emerging infectious diseases and reinforces Uganda's role as a trusted partner in international efforts to develop vaccines and other interventions against epidemic-prone diseases. Dr. Umesh Shaligram, executive director, Serum Institute of India, said:"The initiation of the Phase I clinical study of the ChAdOx1 BDBV vaccine candidate in Uganda is a significant step forward in addressing an important unmet need in Ebola preparedness. The rapid manufacture, stockpiling and supply of investigational doses for clinical evaluation reflect what can be achieved when global collaborators work with urgency and shared purpose. We are pleased to contribute our manufacturing expertise to this collaborative effort and remain committed to supporting the development of innovative vaccines that can help protect communities at risk from emerging infectious diseases worldwide." news.content_title: KMA issues public health advisory on Ebola virus
news.content: The Kenya Medical Association (KMA) has issued a public health advisory on Ebola, urging Kenyans to observe basic hygiene measures, watch for symptoms and seek medical attention early. The association has also assured the public that gatherings remain unrestricted. The advisory comes days after Kenya reported its first imported case of Ebola virus disease caused by the Bundibugyo strain. The Kenyan citizen, who had lived in the Democratic Republic of Congo for seven years, arrived in Kenya through Uganda on October 3 and died on October 5. In a statement, KMA Secretary General Dr Lyndah Kemunto reaffirmed the Ministry of Health's position that there were currently no restrictions on travel, trade, transport or public gatherings. She said weddings, funerals, religious services, conferences, school activities and sporting events could proceed, provided organisers implemented basic hygiene measures, including temperature checks at entry points. “Ebola does not spread through the air. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of a person who is sick with Ebola or has died from it, or with items soiled by those fluids. A person without symptoms does not spread it,” Dr Kemunto said. The association urged Kenyans to follow official Ministry of Health updates, noting that the guidance could change depending on the public health situation. Symptoms of Ebola include sudden fever, headache, muscle pain, weakness, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in some cases, unexplained bleeding. "Because these resemble malaria and typhoid, only a medical assessment and laboratory test can confirm Ebola," Dr Kemunto said. To reduce the risk of infection, the association advised organisers of public events to provide handwashing facilities or sanitiser, conduct temperature checks and designate a person to respond to suspected illnesses and liaise with the nearest health facility. Members of the public were urged to wash their hands frequently, stay at home when unwell, avoid contact with the body fluids of sick people and refrain from sharing personal items such as towels, cups and utensils. KMA also issued precautions for funerals, warning against touching, washing or preparing the body of anyone who dies following a sudden illness accompanied by fever or bleeding. Instead, the public should contact the nearest health facility so authorities can arrange a safe and dignified burial. "If you have travelled from an affected area, have been identified as a contact, or have been near a suspected case, and you develop symptoms, avoid gatherings," Dr Kemunto advised. The association advised people experiencing symptoms to avoid self-medication and urged them to call the Ministry of Health toll-free line at 719 or dial *719# and disclose their travel history to health workers. It also cautioned against stigmatising travellers, health workers and people who had undergone testing, saying fear and discrimination could discourage people from reporting symptoms and increase the risk of transmission. KMA said the rapid detection of Kenya's first imported case and the tracing of contacts demonstrated that the country's public health systems were responding to the threat. The association urged the public to share only verified information as health authorities continue monitoring the situation

She said weddings, funerals, religious services, conferences, school activities and sporting events could proceed, provided organisers implemented basic hygiene measures, including temperature checks at entry points. “Ebola does not spread through the air. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of a person who is sick with Ebola or has died from it, or with items soiled by those fluids. A person without symptoms does not spread it,” Dr Kemunto said. The association urged Kenyans to follow official Ministry of Health updates, noting that the guidance could change depending on the public health situation. Symptoms of Ebola include sudden fever, headache, muscle pain, weakness, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in some cases, unexplained bleeding. "Because these resemble malaria and typhoid, only a medical assessment and laboratory test can confirm Ebola," Dr Kemunto said. To reduce the risk of infection, the association advised organisers of public events to provide handwashing facilities or sanitiser, conduct temperature checks and designate a person to respond to suspected illnesses and liaise with the nearest health facility. Members of the public were urged to wash their hands frequently, stay at home when unwell, avoid contact with the body fluids of sick people and refrain from sharing personal items such as towels, cups and utensils. KMA also issued precautions for funerals, warning against touching, washing or preparing the body of anyone who dies following a sudden illness accompanied by fever or bleeding. Instead, the public should contact the nearest health facility so authorities can arrange a safe and dignified burial. "If you have travelled from an affected area, have been identified as a contact, or have been near a suspected case, and you develop symptoms, avoid gatherings," Dr Kemunto advised. The association advised people experiencing symptoms to avoid self-medication and urged them to call the Ministry of Health toll-free line at 719 or dial *719# and disclose their travel history to health workers. It also cautioned against stigmatising travellers, health workers and people who had undergone testing, saying fear and discrimination could discourage people from reporting symptoms and increase the risk of transmission. KMA said the rapid detection of Kenya's first imported case and the tracing of contacts demonstrated that the country's public health systems were responding to the threat. The association urged the public to share only verified information as health authorities continue monitoring the situation

news.content: News Ebola: What to know about drugs being tested against Bundibugyo virus Joan Mbabazi Saturday, October 10, 2026 The search for effective treatments for Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus is continuing, with researchers investigating medicines that could help patients recover from the disease. ALSO READ: WHO trials new Ebola treatments in DR Congo Unlike Zaire ebolavirus, for which two treatments are approved in the United States, Bundibugyo virus has no specifically approved therapeutics. Patients rely on supportive care, including fluid replacement and treatment of complications, as researchers work to establish which experimental medicines can safely and effectively treat the disease. Here are the drugs being studied and their potential uses. Remdesivir This is an antiviral medicine that interferes with a virus’s ability to make copies of its genetic material. It is being evaluated for its potential to treat Bundibugyo virus disease. The World Health Organization (WHO) has prioritised remdesivir for clinical trials involving confirmed cases. Researchers are also assessing whether combining it with monoclonal antibodies could improve its effectiveness. Although remdesivir is approved for certain other viral infections, it is not approved as a treatment for Bundibugyo virus disease. Its effectiveness against this strain in humans has yet to be established. Remdesivir was developed by Gilead Sciences. In July 2026, the company announced a donation of more than 2,000 vials for the WHO-supported PARTNERS trial, as well as a donation for emergency use in Uganda. Maftivimab Maftivimab is a monoclonal antibody, a laboratory-produced protein designed to recognise and bind to a specific target. It targets a protein on the surface of the Ebola virus, potentially preventing the virus from entering human cells. It is one of three antibodies in Inmazeb, a treatment approved in the United States for Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus. WHO has prioritised maftivimab for clinical evaluation against Bundibugyo virus. However, its effectiveness against this strain has not been established in clinical trials. Maftivimab is one of the antibodies in Inmazeb, developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. MBP134 This is an experimental treatment made up of two monoclonal antibodies designed to recognise Ebola virus proteins and prevent the virus from infecting human cells. Laboratory and animal studies have shown promising activity against several Ebola virus species, including Bundibugyo virus. However, its effectiveness in humans has yet to be established. WHO has prioritised MBP134 for clinical trials to assess its potential to improve survival among patients with Bundibugyo virus disease. It has not been approved for use against Ebola. MBP134 is being developed by Mapp Biopharmaceutical with support from the US Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA). The US Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response has confirmed that investigational doses are being transferred for potential use in the DR Congo and Uganda. Obeldesivir Obeldesivir is an experimental oral antiviral being investigated for post-exposure prophylaxis, which involves giving medicine to people exposed to a virus before they develop symptoms to determine whether it can prevent illness. WHO has selected obeldesivir for clinical evaluation among contacts of confirmed or probable Bundibugyo Ebola cases. The medicine has not been approved for preventing or treating the disease. Obeldesivir was developed by Gilead Sciences. Opaganib Opaganib is an experimental oral medicine that targets processes in human cells that viruses use to enter and multiply, rather than acting directly on the virus. Preclinical studies found that opaganib inhibited Ebola virus activity in human immune cells called macrophages. The studies also found increased survival in one of two animal models and a potentially beneficial effect when the drug was combined with remdesivir. These findings are preliminary and do not establish whether opaganib is effective against Ebola in humans. The drug has not been approved for Ebola treatment. Clinical trial results involving patients with severe COVID-19 have also been reported, but findings from that trial concern a different disease and do not establish that opaganib reduces deaths among Ebola patients. Opaganib is being developed by RedHill Biopharma, which reported the preliminary Ebola findings in June 2026. Inmazeb Inmazeb combines three monoclonal antibodies, namely atoltivimab, maftivimab and odesivimab. Administered intravenously, it binds to proteins on the surface of Zaire ebolavirus, preventing the virus from invading human cells. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Inmazeb for adults and children with Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus. It is not approved for Bundibugyo virus disease, and its effectiveness against this strain has not been established through clinical evidence.The medicine was developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. Ebanga This is a monoclonal antibody treatment administered intravenously. It binds to a protein on the surface of Ebola virus, preventing it from infecting human cells. The US FDA has approved it for adults and children with Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus. However, it is not approved for Bundibugyo virus disease, and its effectiveness against this strain has not been established. Ebanga was developed by Ridgeback Biotherapeutics under licence from the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID). Emergent BioSolutions handles its manufacturing, sales and distribution in the United States and Canada, while Ridgeback serves as its global access partner. The treatment is available free of charge in Ebola-affected countries through its access programme. Maftivimab Maftivimab is a monoclonal antibody, a laboratory-produced protein designed to recognise and bind to a specific target. It targets a protein on the surface of the Ebola virus, potentially preventing the virus from entering human cells. It is one of three antibodies in Inmazeb, a treatment approved in the United States for Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus. WHO has prioritised maftivimab for clinical evaluation against Bundibugyo virus. However, its effectiveness against this strain has not been established in clinical trials. Maftivimab is one of the antibodies in Inmazeb, developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. MBP134 This is an experimental treatment made up of two monoclonal antibodies designed to recognise Ebola virus proteins and prevent the virus from infecting human cells. Laboratory and animal studies have shown promising activity against several Ebola virus species, including Bundibugyo virus. However, its effectiveness in humans has yet to be established. WHO has prioritised MBP134 for clinical trials to assess its potential to improve survival among patients with Bundibugyo virus disease. It has not been approved for use against Ebola. MBP134 is being developed by Mapp Biopharmaceutical with support from the US Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority (BARDA). The US Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response has confirmed that investigational doses are being transferred for potential use in the DR Congo and Uganda. Obeldesivir Obeldesivir is an experimental oral antiviral being investigated for post-exposure prophylaxis, which involves giving medicine to people exposed to a virus before they develop symptoms to determine whether it can prevent illness. WHO has selected obeldesivir for clinical evaluation among contacts of confirmed or probable Bundibugyo Ebola cases. The medicine has not been approved for preventing or treating the disease. Obeldesivir was developed by Gilead Sciences. Opaganib Opaganib is an experimental oral medicine that targets processes in human cells that viruses use to enter and multiply, rather than acting directly on the virus. Preclinical studies found that opaganib inhibited Ebola virus activity in human immune cells called macrophages. The studies also found increased survival in one of two animal models and a potentially beneficial effect when the drug was combined with remdesivir. These findings are preliminary and do not establish whether opaganib is effective against Ebola in humans. The drug has not been approved for Ebola treatment. Clinical trial results involving patients with severe COVID-19 have also been reported, but findings from that trial concern a different disease and do not establish that opaganib reduces deaths among Ebola patients. Opaganib is being developed by RedHill Biopharma, which reported the preliminary Ebola findings in June 2026. Inmazeb Inmazeb combines three monoclonal antibodies, namely atoltivimab, maftivimab and odesivimab. Administered intravenously, it binds to proteins on the surface of Zaire ebolavirus, preventing the virus from invading human cells. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Inmazeb for adults and children with Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus. It is not approved for Bundibugyo virus disease, and its effectiveness against this strain has not been established through clinical evidence.The medicine was developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. Ebanga This is a monoclonal antibody treatment administered intravenously. It binds to a protein on the surface of Ebola virus, preventing it from infecting human cells. The US FDA has approved it for adults and children with Ebola disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus. However, it is not approved for Bundibugyo virus disease, and its effectiveness against this strain has not been established. Ebanga was developed by Ridgeback Biotherapeutics under licence from the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID). Emergent BioSolutions handles its manufacturing, sales and distribution in the United States and Canada, while Ridgeback serves as its global access partner. The treatment is available free of charge in Ebola-affected countries through its access programme. news.content_title: What is Bundibugyo virus disease and why is it lethal?
news.content: Until very recently, many Kenyans had not heard of Bundibugyo and those who had probably never paid much attention to it until Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale announced on October 5 that Kenya had confirmed its first-ever Ebola case. Many know Ebola, as the name has been around for decades, but Bundibugyo has become a trending topic, with online discussions seeking to understand why it is attracting so much attention. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), Bundibugyo is a rare Ebola virus strain with reported outbreaks across East and Central Africa. The outbreak originally began in May 2026 in Ituri province, a northeastern region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). It has since exploded into the largest Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak ever recorded, topping 8,700 confirmed cases and more than 4,200 deaths. Kenya became the fourth country in the region to deal with cases, triggering neighbouring nations such as Uganda, which was declared Ebola-free in August, to put their health systems on high alert. Kenya's lone case was a citizen who had been living in the DRC for seven years and had travelled by land through Uganda before boarding a domestic commercial flight to Nairobi on the night of October 3. Duale said the patient had been infected a month earlier and received treatment in the DRC before travelling, but tragically died days later while receiving treatment at Nairobi Hospital. WHO says Bundibugyo is a severe and often fatal form of Ebola virus disease, with fruit bats suspected to be its natural reservoirs. "Human infection occurs through broken skin or eyes, nose, mouth when handling infected animals, monkeys or bushmeat," WHO said. The disease is not airborne and spreads from person to person through direct contact with the bodily fluids of symptomatic individuals. It takes between two and 21 days for symptoms to appear, and people are not contagious until they actually feel sick. Early signs resemble those of common flu, including fever, fatigue, body aches, headache and sore throat, making the disease difficult to diagnose early. "Later signs worsen to stomach issues, organ failure and sometimes internal and external bleeding," WHO says. The organisation says the disease can only be confirmed through laboratory tests, such as PCR or antibody tests, because its symptoms resemble those of malaria and other tropical diseases. WHO says stopping the spread of the virus requires quick action, including rapid isolation, contact tracing and safe burials. The organisation has advised the public to wash their hands often with soap and water, avoid touching anyone who is sick or their bodily fluids, and seek medical care early at a health facility if unwell. People handling deceased bodies, including healthcare workers without protective gear, are at the greatest risk of infection. "Once identified, protective measures including proper PPE, disinfection and isolation are highly effective," WHO said. The Bundibugyo Ebola virus is particularly concerning because, unlike the more common Zaire strain, there is currently no approved vaccine or virus-specific treatment. Medical teams are relying entirely on intensive supportive care and emergency, early-stage clinical drug trials. Although the current outbreak was reported in the DRC, the virus strain was first discovered in 2007 in the Bundibugyo District of western Uganda. Public anxiety is elevated as health authorities in Kenya and Uganda aggressively trace dozens of high-risk contacts. These include medical staff who treated the deceased patient, family members and the 23 passengers and four crew members who shared the Jambojet flight from Kampala to Nairobi. On Wednesday, Duale said 57 people linked to the deceased patient had been identified and were being managed in accordance with established health protocols

news.content_zh: 本文讨论了邦迪布古病毒,这是一种罕见的埃博拉病毒病病毒株,曾在刚果民主共和国(DRC)引发了暴发疫情,并传播至肯尼亚。肯尼亚首次确认的病例于2026年10月5日公布,涉及一名曾在DRC居住七年、经乌干达后抵达内罗毕的公民。该患者一个月前在DRC被感染,并接受了治疗治疗,于2026年10月8日在内罗毕医院去世。世界卫生组织(WHO)报告称,邦迪布古病毒是一种严重且常致命的疾病,目前尚无批准的疫苗或治疗治疗方案,且通过与有症状个体的体液直接接触传播。该暴发疫情始于2026年5月,在Ituri省爆发,目前已确认超过8,700例病例,死亡人数超过4,200人。肯尼亚和乌干达的卫生当局正在追踪接触者,包括医疗人员、家庭成员以及Jambojet航班上的乘客,以防止进一步传播。WHO建议采取防护措施,如使用个人防护装备(PPE)、消毒和隔离,以控制该病毒。

analysis_zh.time: 该暴发疫情始于2026年5月,肯尼亚首次确认病例是在2026年10月5日。患者于2026年10月8日在内罗毕医院接受治疗治疗时去世。文章发布日期为2026年10月9日。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该暴发疫情起源于DRC的Ituri省,并传播至肯尼亚。患者是一名在DRC居住七年、经乌干达后抵达内罗毕的肯尼亚公民。受影响的人群包括患者本人、医疗工作者、家庭成员以及从坎帕拉飞往内罗毕的Jambojet航班上的23名乘客和4名机组人员。
analysis_zh.event: 肯尼亚于2026年10月5日确认了其首例邦迪布古病毒病病例,该病例是在内罗毕医院于2026年10月8日患者去世后公布的。世界卫生组织(WHO)报告称,邦迪布古病毒是一种罕见的埃博拉病毒病毒株,在东非和中非地区引发了暴发疫情。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 在DRC的暴发疫情已确认超过8,700例病例,死亡人数超过4,200人。邦迪布古病毒是一种严重且常致命的病毒,目前尚无批准的疫苗或治疗治疗方案。它通过与有症状个体的体液直接接触传播,且不具备空气传播能力。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 肯尼亚和乌干达的卫生当局正在积极追踪接触者,包括医疗人员、家庭成员以及Jambojet航班上的乘客。WHO强调需要快速隔离、接触追踪和安全埋葬。患者的病例通过实验室检测确认,且正在实施防护措施。

Pylori Norovirus Healthcare Associated Infections (HAI) Prevention Antibiotics Immunizations Vaccines Respiratory Infections Community-Acquired Pneumonia Measles Influenza Sexually Transmitted Diseases HIV / AIDS HPV HSV PrEP Skin & Soft Tissue Diseases MRSA Zoonotic & Vector-Borne Diseases Lyme Disease ZIKA Choose Topic Spotlight - Vaccines in America| Antibiotics Deconstructed| Bench to Bedside With SIDP| Antimicrobial Stewardship| Hepatitis Advertisement News|Articles|October 11, 2026 Ebola Update: DRC Outbreak Passes 8,700 Cases and 4,200 Deaths Advertisement The CDC reported 8,750 confirmed cases of Ebola disease and 4,208 confirmed deaths as of October 6, 2026, in an outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).1 The agency said the outbreak is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest on record. This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC.1 It surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation, compared with approximately 235 days for the 2018 DRC outbreak to pass the same mark. Case Counts, Geographic Spread, and Cross-Border Cases The DRC accounts for 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 confirmed deaths, with no probable cases or deaths included in the official DRC Ministry of Health reporting.1 Cases have been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Sud-Ubangi, and Tshopo provinces. South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. Outside the DRC, Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases, 2 confirmed deaths, 1 probable case, and 1 probable death, with cases reported in the capital of Kampala.1 Kenya reported 1 confirmed case and 1 confirmed death, and France reported 1 confirmed case with no deaths. The last confirmed case in Uganda recovered and was released from care on July 16, 2026, and the last case in France was released on July 4, 2026.1 CDC reports no active cases in either country. Suspected cases and deaths in the DRC have been temporarily excluded from the count pending investigations and data standardization. Learn More Clinical Insights and the Geopolitics Surrounding the Ongoing Ebola Outbreak Response Challenges, Travel Restrictions, and US Risk CDC cited limited health infrastructure, ongoing conflict, violence against health care workers, shortages of personal protective equipment, frequent population movement, and misinformation as factors complicating the response.1 Health care workers are becoming infected while treating patients. The agency warned cross-border travel increases the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and other areas. To reduce the risk of importation, the US has temporarily restricted entry for travelers who were in the DRC within 21 days of their flight, including US citizens, who will not be allowed to board commercial flights with US destinations.1 Citizens and nationals present in Uganda or South Sudan, and not the DRC, within 21 days must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces (Level 4) and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces (Level 3).1 A Level 2 notice advises enhanced precautions in the DRC and Uganda.2 No Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the US, and CDC considers the overall risk to the American public and travelers low. About 500 CDC staff are involved in the response, including more than 120 people deployed to affected countries.1 CDC is working internationally and domestically to prevent Ebola from entering the US. Frequently Asked Questions What virus is causing the current Ebola outbreak in the DRC? The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus. CDC describes it as the 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC. Is there a risk of Ebola in the United States? No Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the US, and CDC considers the likelihood of spread to the US very low. The agency has temporarily restricted entry for travelers recently in the DRC. Which areas should travelers avoid? CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces in the DRC and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces. Travelers to other parts of the DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions and monitor for symptoms for 21 days after leaving. References Ebola Outbreak: Current Situation. CDC.
