Outside the DRC, Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases, 2 confirmed deaths, 1 probable case, and 1 probable death, with cases reported in the capital of Kampala.1 Kenya reported 1 confirmed case and 1 confirmed death, and France reported 1 confirmed case with no deaths. The last confirmed case in Uganda recovered and was released from care on July 16, 2026, and the last case in France was released on July 4, 2026.1 CDC reports no active cases in either country. Suspected cases and deaths in the DRC have been temporarily excluded from the count pending investigations and data standardization. Learn More Clinical Insights and the Geopolitics Surrounding the Ongoing Ebola Outbreak Response Challenges, Travel Restrictions, and US Risk CDC cited limited health infrastructure, ongoing conflict, violence against health care workers, shortages of personal protective equipment, frequent population movement, and misinformation as factors complicating the response.1 Health care workers are becoming infected while treating patients. The agency warned cross-border travel increases the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and other areas. To reduce the risk of importation, the US has temporarily restricted entry for travelers who were in the DRC within 21 days of their flight, including US citizens, who will not be allowed to board commercial flights with US destinations.1 Citizens and nationals present in Uganda or South Sudan, and not the DRC, within 21 days must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces (Level 4) and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces (Level 3).1 A Level 2 notice advises enhanced precautions in the DRC and Uganda.2 No Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the US, and CDC considers the overall risk to the American public and travelers low. About 500 CDC staff are involved in the response, including more than 120 people deployed to affected countries.1 CDC is working internationally and domestically to prevent Ebola from entering the US. Frequently Asked Questions What virus is causing the current Ebola outbreak in the DRC? The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus. CDC describes it as the 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC. Is there a risk of Ebola in the United States? No Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the US, and CDC considers the likelihood of spread to the US very low. The agency has temporarily restricted entry for travelers recently in the DRC. Which areas should travelers avoid? CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces in the DRC and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces. Travelers to other parts of the DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions and monitor for symptoms for 21 days after leaving. References Ebola Outbreak: Current Situation. CDC. news.content_title: Phase II Clinical Trial of NV-387 Oral Gummies as Treatment of Ebola Progressing Well, Says NanoViricides
news.content: Skip to content This page contains press release content distributed by XPR Media. Members of the editorial and news staff of the USA TODAY Network were not involved in the creation of this content. The placement of this content is part of a paid service. Phase II Clinical Trial of NV-387 Oral Gummies as Treatment of Ebola Progressing Well, Says NanoViricides NanoViricides SHELTON, CT / ACCESS Newswire / October 13, 2026 / NanoViricides, Inc. (NYSE American:NNVC) (the “Company”), a clinical stage leader developing antiviral drugs that viruses cannot escape, said today that its Phase IIA Ebola Treatment Clinical Trial of NV-387 Oral Gummies is progressing well. The Phase IIA part of the clinical trial is designed to evaluate different dosage regimens of the oral gummies for the treatment of different severity levels of the Ebola Bundibugyo virus infection and disease in the current Ebola Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (“DRC”). The trial is enrolling and is expected to continue enrolling persons exhibiting different disease severity levels, in the “Dry Stage” and “Wet Stage”. The clinical symptoms of the Ebola BDBV disease are complex, and possibly different from prior Ebola virus outbreaks, as explained in the footnote i. Patients are known to come to the Ebola Treatment Centers only when they feel severely ill. Therefore, we are anticipating mostly “Wet Stage” patients, with severe vomiting and diarrhea, to be the primarily enrolled population. Some patients may not be able to take the oral gummies due to vomiting bouts and may be withdrawn; such subjects would not be considered as evaluable if enrolled. The Phase IIA part of the trial is designed to examine the safety and tolerability of NV-387 oral gummies dosing in the Ebola patients, and the number of days that the drug is tolerated within the context of the disease, starting at 6 days of dosing, and extending by 3 day increments to a maximum of 12 days of treatment. The NV-387 treatment will be stopped when the patient’s viral load has become undetectable based on qRT-PCR. Efficacy is not expected to be evaluated in a scientific, statistically significant, manner in such an adaptive treatment scenario. Therefore, and with due ethical consideration, a parallel group of no NV-387 treatment is excluded in this exploratory Phase IIA part. Nevertheless, an efficacy signal can be seen even in this small clinical trial with up to 20 subjects, if NV-387 is highly effective. This can happen if the data of 20 subjects treated with NV-387 is found to be sufficient to statistically discriminate the NV-387 treated group from the general observations of treatment of Ebola patients in the Ebola Treatment Centers in the same area. Ebola Patients in this area have generally experienced an infection-to-fatality rate (IFR) of 67% to 75%. The IFR corrects the data for the fact that the infected person dies on an average about three weeks later, and therefore is a more accurate representation of reality than the crude Case Fatality Rate (CFR) ii. The Company will be able to make an announcement regarding (i) whether NV-387 is found to be sufficiently safe and well tolerated to continue into Phase IIB, and, (ii) if NV-387 group is well discriminated from the general expectation of 67-75% IFR, then whether NV-387 oral gummies treatment demonstrated signs of efficacy against the Ebola Bundibugyo virus; after the Phase IIA clinical trial is completed and a report is prepared by the Principal Investigator’s team for formal communication. After an appropriate NV-387 Oral Gummies dosage regimen is identified, it will be used in an expanded, randomized, controlled clinical trial, Part IIB, to evaluate effectiveness of the Oral treatment drug NV-387 Oral Gummies. NV-387 is designed to attack the virus and reduce the viral load in the body. Reducing viral load correlates with improvement in physiological function. Reduction in viral load to undetected level means complete recovery from the viral disease. However, the bodily functions, may take longer time even after reaching undetectable viral load, as the virus-attacked organs rejuvenate. It is also possible that some permanent damage, e.g. kidney damage, may persist even after virological recovery. The current BDBV outbreak has continued to expand, with 9,000 confirmed cases and 4,339 deaths as of October 10, 2026, according to the WHO iii, with all but a few cases in DRC. An Ebola patient was able to travel from DRC via Uganda to Kenya, and died at home there recently, despite travel restrictions. Fortunately after a week, no secondary infections from this patient have been detected (yet). This emphasizes the potential risk to the world, although the possibility of an Ebola outbreak in the USA or globally remains negligible, because of various global travel restrictions. Within DRC, while the initial outbreak sites including Ituri have possibly stabilized, the outbreak has started gaining strength in Nord Kivu province with 40% of national confirmed cases now coming from Nord Kivu, which does not have sufficient ebola treatment centers capacity, with only 29 beds in treatment center, and only about 20 “transit facility” beds for holding suspected cases until diagnosis results come in, according to Doctors Without Borders iv. Recently, thousands of refugees fled from a refugee camp where more than 30 people had died from Ebola BDBV, to escape from security forces that were investigating weapons stored in the camp. Their fleeing has increased the risk of spread v. Additionally, 6 new Ebola cases were recorded in an Eastern part of DRC controlled by rebel groups, further complicating efforts to control the outbreak vi. The USA has been, laudably, and proudly, the largest provider of humanitarian and relief assistance in this outbreak, with almost $1.4 Billion in contributions. The USA has already provided $887 Million, and has pledged another $500 Million, of which $267 million has been released, according to the US Department of State vii. There is no current threat of Ebola in the USA. The US Government is active in ensuring that suspected or confirmed ebolavirus cases do not enter the general population in the USA. To this end, travel from DRC has been restricted, with pre-travel quarantine requirements imposed, and suspect travelers are directed to screening at specific airports and may be further quarantined. Travelers going to and from Central Africa need to constantly check travel restrictions as well as travel limitations in light of these changing outbreak conditions. It is apparent that travel restrictions have been able to control the outbreak periphery to DRC alone (with few early cases in Uganda) minimizing risk to the rest of the world. There is no approved Treatment or Vaccine for the new variant of the Bundibugyo Ebolavirus (BDBV) that is causing the current rapidly expanding outbreak of the Ebolavirus Disease (EVD) in DRC. The rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola virus causing the current outbreak appears to be its new variant, likely freshly introduced from some animal source viii, such as fruit bats. NV-387 is a broad-spectrum antiviral that mimics the host-side features that the virus requires, and is likely to be effective against Ebola viruses because they use the same host-side feature mimicked by NV-387. NV-387 Oral Gummies is a drug product readily delivered orally. It does not even require swallowing effort or water, because it dissolves in the mouth by itself, simplifying delivery for even sick individuals with swallowing difficulties. This oral delivery is an important feature that puts NV-387, a broad-spectrum antiviral, as being superior to the other approaches. “Only safe and effective broad-spectrum antiviral drugs like NV-387 that can effectively tackle most viral infections will enable the world to combat viruses and defend the global population in the war against known and unknown nanoscopic enemies that are viruses,” commented Dr. Diwan, adding, “Today, NV-387 is the only drug in clinical development with such broad-spectrum potential that promises to combat diverse epidemics like Mpox and Ebola, and even Measles, to the best of our knowledge.” The outbreak which was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (“PHEIC”) by the WHO on May 17, 2026, continues to rapidly expand, outpacing containment efforts. The outbreak arose in a high traffic region bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with travel contacts to Uganda, and South Sudan and with 11 more nations in Africa at risk ix. NV-387 is a broad-spectrum antiviral that mimics the host-side feature called heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG) that over 90-95% of human pathogenic viruses require for infecting cells. No matter how much the virus changes in the field, it continues to use HSPG, and therefore it cannot escape the drug NV-387. In contrast, Remdesivir is a small molecule inhibitor of the viral RDRP enzyme needed for making copies of the viral genome, and the virus can possibly escape by small number of mutations. All Ebola viruses utilize HSPG as the attachment receptor prior to gaining entry into the cell. Thereafter, followed by entry into the cell inside endosomes, the ebolavirus surface glycoprotein is substantially degraded, opening up its site for binding to its cognate receptor called NPC1, thereby entering into the cytoplasm where the next steps in its replication begin. Thus there is a strong rationale that NV-387 could be highly effective against Ebola virus infections, not just Bundibugyo, but also the Sudan and other viruses for which there are no treatments. All previous anti-Ebola efforts have been focused on vaccines and antibodies x. This has led to approval of therapies that are specific to the Ebolavirus Zaire strain only, albeit with limited effectiveness. This leaves out all other filoviruses of consequence: Sudan, Marburg, and the more rare Bundibugyo with no treatment or vaccine. In contrast, if NV-387, as a broad-spectrum antiviral, is found to be effective against the Bundibugyo virus, it will likely be effective against all ebolaviruses and possibly all filoviruses; that would be a game changer for pandemic preparedness. At present, BDBV has been consistently demonstrating high crude CFR of 48% and IFR of 67% in DRC. Therefore, BDBV is of great concern as a potential pandemic disease. However, it is believed that ebolaviruses do not transmit via respiratory droplets or aerosols and rather require extensive contact with bodily fluids of an infected person. In addition, within DRC and internationally, certain protective quarantine measures for travel from the outbreak areas have been implemented. Therefore, currently there is no apparent threat of a global pandemic. With ever-increasing global travel, local outbreaks such as ebola can quickly travel far and wide potentially causing global pandemics, as was the case with COVID-19, if not caught in time. It is not feasible to produce a new vaccine and a new set of antibody drugs to combat every possible virus. Even if vaccines and antibodies are produced, the virus would escape by generating variants, as the world has witnessed during the COVID-19 pandemic. ABOUT NANOVIRICIDES NanoViricides, Inc. (NYSE American:NNVC) (the “Company”), a clinical stage leader developing antiviral drugs that viruses cannot escape, said today that its Phase IIA Ebola Treatment Clinical Trial of NV-387 Oral Gummies is progressing well. The Phase IIA part of the clinical trial is designed to evaluate different dosage regimens of the oral gummies for the treatment of different severity levels of the Ebola Bundibugyo virus infection and disease in the current Ebola Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (“DRC”). The trial is enrolling and is expected to continue enrolling persons exhibiting different disease severity levels, in the “Dry Stage” and “Wet Stage”. Patients are known to come to the Ebola Treatment Centers only when they feel severely ill. The NV-387 treatment will be stopped when the patient’s viral load has become undetectable based on qRT-PCR. Efficacy is not expected to be evaluated in a scientific, statistically significant, manner in such an adaptive treatment scenario. Therefore, and with due ethical consideration, a parallel group of no NV-387 treatment is excluded in this exploratory Phase IIA part. Nevertheless, an efficacy signal can be seen even in this small clinical trial with up to 20 subjects, if NV-387 is highly effective. This can happen if the data of 20 subjects treated with NV-387 is found to be sufficient to statistically discriminate the NV-387 treated group from the general observations of treatment of Ebola patients in the Ebola Treatment Centers in the same area. It is also possible that some permanent damage, e.g. kidney damage, may persist even after virological recovery. news.title_zh: NV-387口香糖二期临床试验作为埃博拉病毒治疗进展顺利,NanoViricides公司称
news.source_body_en: NanoViricides, Inc. reported on October 13, 2026, that its Phase II clinical trial of NV-387 oral gummies as a treatment for Ebola Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) infection in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is progressing well. The trial is designed to assess the safety and tolerability of the drug in patients with varying disease severity levels, particularly those in the 'Wet Stage' with severe vomiting and diarrhea. The trial does not include a parallel control group, so efficacy cannot be evaluated in a statistically significant manner. As of October 10, 2026, the DRC outbreak has resulted in 9,000 confirmed cases and 4,339 deaths, with an infection-to-fatality rate (IFR) of 67% to 75%. The US Government is actively preventing the spread of ebolavirus to the general population through travel restrictions and has provided over $1.4 billion in humanitarian assistance. The trial will continue to enroll patients and will determine whether NV-387 is safe enough to proceed to Phase IIB, where its effectiveness will be evaluated in a randomized, controlled setting.

supplementary_news.content: 24/7 LivePhiladelphiaPennsylvaniaNew JerseyDelaware 72° Ebola US doctor infected with Ebola critically ill but says he is 'cautiously optimistic' The doctor's family, including his wife and four kids, will join him in Germany. The American doctor who contracted Ebola has arrived in Germany and is receiving care, according to the missionary group he works for. ByMorgan Winsor, David Brennan, Youri Benadjaoud and Mary Kekatos Friday, May 22, 2026 Share The American doctor infected with Ebola said he is "cautiously optimistic" about his health improving amid more severe symptoms. Dr. Peter Stafford contracted the disease while working with patients in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He was evacuated to Germany to receive specialty care and is currently hospitalized at Charite University Hospital in Berlin. "Before I was evacuated I was feeling really concerned I wasn't going to make it, and now I'm cautiously optimistic," Stafford said in a press release from Serge, the international Christian missionary group that employs him. His colleague, Dr. Scott Myhre, Serge area director for East and Central Africa, said Stafford is critically ill but feeling better than he did on Wednesday, and is able to eat small amounts of food. Stafford initially experienced what are known as "dry" symptoms such as fever, aches and fatigue. RELATED: WHO chief concerned over 'scale and speed' of Ebola outbreak However, he is currently experiencing "wet" symptoms including vomiting and diarrhea. Myhre said Stafford's laboratory reports are "trending slightly in the right direction." "Peter has also received two intravenous treatments designed to improve Ebola outcomes," Myhre said in the press release. "The German care teams rotate in three-hour shifts since they must wear full-body hazmat suits as they care for him. We're thankful for their dedication and expertise." On Wednesday, Stafford's colleague, Matt Allison, executive director of Serge, told ABC News that the doctor has been receiving monoclonal antibodies during his hospitalization. Stafford's wife, Dr. Rebekah Stafford, and their four children landed in Berlin at 10 p.m. local time Wednesday and have been moved into a separate space at Charite University Hospital. All are asymptomatic and will continue to isolate and be monitored, according to Serge. The organization added that Stafford's family is able to see him through a window. Meanwhile, another Serge missionary physician, Dr. Patrick LaRochelle, is currently at Bulovka Hospital in Prague. He is quarantine and remains asymptomatic, Serge said. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday announced new arrival restrictions for flights carrying people who were recently in Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda or South Sudan amid the Ebola outbreak in the region. Flights will be ordered to land at Washington-Dulles Airport in Virginia, the notice said, where "enhanced public health measures are being implemented." A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told ABC News that Air France boarded a passenger from the Democratic Republic of Congo "in error" on a flight to the United States. The flight was initially bound for Detroit and was diverted to Montreal. "Due to entry restrictions put in place to reduce the risk of the Ebola virus, the passenger should not have boarded the plane," the spokesperson said. The Ebola outbreak in the eastern DRC had caused 139 suspected deaths with nearly 600 suspected cases as of Wednesday, according to the latest update from World Health Organization Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. RELATED: 'We're working on it': Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Ebola, hantavirus response Tedros said cases of Ebola have been reported in several urban areas of the eastern DRC amid the ongoing outbreak, including the major cities of Goma and Bunia, and that at least two cases and one death have been recorded in neighboring Uganda's capital, Kampala. Cases have also been reported among health workers, according to Ghebreyesus. At least 51 cases have so far been confirmed in the ongoing outbreak. The DHS flight restriction notice said that while South Sudan has not reported any confirmed cases in the current outbreak, "It is considered at high risk because of its close border with affected areas in eastern DRC and Uganda, limited healthcare infrastructure and cross-border population movement." The outbreak was first detected in the DRC's northeastern province of Ituri, with cases officially confirmed by the health ministry on May 15. It marks the 17th outbreak of Ebola virus disease in the DRC, which is Africa's second-largest country and its fourth-most populous nation. The WHO convened an emergency committee on Tuesday night, following Tedros' declaration of a public health emergency of international concern on Sunday -- one level below a pandemic in the United Nations agency's alert system. It was the first time a WHO chief had declared such an emergency before convening the emergency committee. After the meeting, the committee agreed that the outbreak did not meet the criteria of a pandemic emergency, which was applied to the global COVID-19 outbreak. Anais Legand, the WHO's technical officer for viral hemorrhagic fevers, said on Wednesday that the Ebola outbreak may have started a couple of months ago and that investigations are ongoing. "Our priority is really to cut the transmission chain by implementing contact tracing, isolating and caring for all suspects and confirmed cases," she said. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare variant of Ebola for which there are no approved vaccines or therapeutics and which requires different diagnostics than other variants. Case fatality rates for previous Bundibugyo outbreaks have ranged from 30% to 50%, according to the WHO. Dr. Satish K. Pillai, incident manager for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Ebola response, confirmed at a CDC press conference on Tuesday that genetic testing from this outbreak shows it is similar to the "genetic fingerprints" from outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, meaning there are diagnostic tools available that can detect this strain of Ebola. Pillai said on Monday that the agency had activated its Emergency Operations Center through its country offices in the DRC and in Uganda, and is deploying technical experts that have been requested from Atlanta headquarters. The risk to the U.S. general public remains low, Pillai said. Also on Monday, the CDC introduced entry restrictions on non-U.S. passport holders that had been in Uganda, the DRC or South Sudan in the previous 21 days before attempted entry into the U.S. ABC News' Luke Barr, Eric M. supplementary_news.content: Sterile processing professionals face constant interruptions, cognitive overload, increasingly complex devices, and hundreds of IFUs. Randalyn Harreld, CRCST, FHSPA, explains why health care organizations must address the human factors behind SPD performance rather than expecting frontline professionals to simply absorb ever-increasing complexity. In this podcast with ICT, Danielle Updegraff, MBA, BSN, RN, discusses real-time location systems, which can give infection prevention teams greater visibility into hand hygiene, workflow, and infectious disease exposures, but sustainable improvement still depends on staff engagement, leadership, education, and culture. In this complete interview, ICT speaks with Endale Tilahun, MD, MPH, about a Malawi community program that reduced missed HIV testing and achieved 0.2% positivity among exposed infants through household follow-up, individualized case management, and coordinated health and social support. Environmental testing found bacterial contamination on many lead garments and described what lead garment cleaning technicians routinely encounter during servicing. New research presented at AIDS 2026 indicates that 2-drug HIV regimens and long-acting injectable therapies are effective treatment options that also enhance personalized care. Investigators highlight that shared decision-making, adherence, quality of life, and minimizing long-term medication exposure are becoming more vital alongside maintaining viral suppression. International infection prevention leaders discuss how Ireland and Saudi Arabia educate, recruit, and prepare IPC professionals while advocating for broader, multidisciplinary career pathways worldwide. A hantavirus outbreak linked to a South American cruise ship is drawing global attention, but experts say fears of a COVID-19-style pandemic are largely unsupported. Infectious disease physician Matthew Pullen, MD, discusses Andes virus transmission, misinformation, cruise ship risks, and what health care professionals should really be watching for. The cohosts of Contagious Conversation speak with Tori Whitacre Martonicz, lead editor of Infection Control Today, about her presentation at the SoCal SPA Spring Conference, and how the conference speakers emphasized leadership beyond titles, urging SPD professionals to share knowledge, speak up, and turn everyday insights into safer patient care practices. Dental assistants manage sterilization, infection control, and patient education—yet most states require zero formal training. They earn the lowest wages in dental offices. Meet Sherrie Busby's 42-year mission to secure standardized credentialing and fair recognition. (Audio podcast) As her 2025 APIC presidency concludes, Carol McLay, DrPH, MPH, RN, CIC, FAPIC, FSHEA, discusses public health funding cuts, science advocacy, global partnerships, workforce development, and why infection preventionists must speak up. In this exclusive ICT interview, she shares lessons from a tumultuous year and her vision for strengthening the infection prevention profession worldwide. Missing instruments and processing delays can strain OR–SPD relationships. At AORN 2026, John Kimsey, vice president of processing optimization and customer success for STERIS, discusses understanding root causes, exploring off-site reprocessing for ambulatory surgical centers, and using hands-on simulation to help surgical teams see sterile processing from a different perspective. This week's coverage in Infection Control Today centered on a common thread: the systems, partnerships, and data that let infection prevention teams catch problems before patients are harmed. UPMC’s genomic surveillance initiative earned national recognition for patient safety. Alexander Sundermann, DrPH, CIC, FAPIC, AL-CIP, explains how the award could help infection preventionists secure leadership support and sustainable funding for earlier outbreak detection. Knowing the protocol is only the beginning. In The Clean Bite, Sherrie Busby explores how explaining the why, addressing staff concerns, and creating clear procedures can help dental teams make infection control part of everyday practice. What might infection prevention rounds miss when visible conditions dominate the conversation? Tommy Davis, PhD, CMIP, a member of ICT's executive advisory board, makes the case for structured observations of clinical workflows, shared accountability, and greater attention to environmental services staff’s insights. A proposed $27.7 million reduction in AHRQ funding raises questions about support for infection prevention research and implementation. Here is what the September 25 announcement identifies, as well as what remains unknown about specific IPC programs. Two posters presented by Karen Jones, MPH, RN, CIC, FAPIC, at the APIC Annual Conference and Exposition examine surveillance responsibilities and staffing in small hospitals, as well as IPs’ reported experiences after implementing electronic surveillance. Findings highlight opportunities for more investigation, rounding, and communication. A followed procedure can still leave patients at risk if it no longer matches validated requirements. Annetta L. McKnight, MHA, BSN, CRCST, CER, examines how infection prevention and sterile processing can identify process drift, assess disruptions, and strengthen shared oversight of medical device reprocessing. Artist and designer Matthew Caliman shares how personal loss inspired the Cleanup Crew, a handwashing education project using cartoon faucets, songs, and games to help families revisit an essential health message. In 1926, Karen Jones’s grandmother lost 5 children to measles in 8 days. A century later, Jones connects that devastating family history to vaccination, outbreak preparedness, and the role of infection preventionists in building trust. What Were the Biggest Infection Prevention Stories This Week? Ebola's Outpaced Response, Lyme Coinfection Data, and Sterile Processing Burnout Explained, and more The knowledge used to prevent infections can also be misused. Through a personal reflection on gaming, AI, and biological research, an infection preventionist explores why faster answers make human judgment, peer consultation, and accountability increasingly important. A study of 193,260 individuals found overlapping tick-borne antibody levels more frequently among those with Lyme antibodies, highlighting diagnostic challenges when active coinfections are not confirmed. A shifting mask or fogged eyewear can interrupt focus when precision matters most. Dana Weaver Storm, MHA, BSN, RN, examines the challenges of prolonged surgical mask use and how perioperative leaders can support comfort, visibility, and consistent adherence. What happens when one disinfectant cannot satisfy every IFU? At AHE in New Orleans, Diane Cullen discusses weighted risk assessment, documenting difficult decisions, and why infection prevention and EVS need to work together. Turnover pressure can leave critical OR cleaning steps unfinished. Karen deKay, MSN, RN, EBP-C, CNOR, CIC, FAPIC, examines common gaps in environmental hygiene and how shared responsibilities, attention to disinfectant contact time, and ongoing education can help teams strengthen practices between cases. A patient with fever and no recent travel could still have dengue. Florida’s local transmission highlights why clinicians and infection preventionists should look beyond travel history and recognize warning signs. High contact follow-up rates suggest progress, but who is being missed? Inside the DRC’s Ebola response, shortages, strained treatment centers, and gaps in community trust reveal a more complicated story. Sterile processing professionals face constant interruptions, cognitive overload, increasingly complex devices, and hundreds of IFUs. Randalyn Harreld, CRCST, FHSPA, explains why health care organizations must address the human factors behind SPD performance rather than expecting frontline professionals to simply absorb ever-increasing complexity. Long-acting HIV therapies promise greater convenience, but fewer doses alone may not solve adherence or access challenges. Lloyd Bibby and Pooja Goyal, MS(Pharm), discuss patient choice, weekly oral and injectable therapies, health system capacity, equitable access, and the real-world measures that will define success. This week on Infection Control Today, the stories ranged from emerging drug-resistant pathogens circling the globe to a landmark decade of surface science—all against a backdrop of ongoing outbreaks and a hard look at what the profession owes its own workforce. At AHE 2026 in New Orleans, The Beryl Institute's Stacy Palmer discussed 8 guiding principles for experience excellence and why EVS professionals influence far more than environmental cleanliness. Their interactions, workplace culture, and connection with patients help shape the overall human experience of health care. What Is Trichophyton indotineae? Drug-Resistant Ringworm Spreads to 29 Countries Drug-resistant Trichophyton indotineae has now been identified in 29 countries. Its resistance to first-line terbinafine, resemblance to other dermatophytes, and expanding global transmission are creating new challenges for diagnosis, treatment, surveillance, and antifungal stewardship. Infection Control Today celebrates 30 years of covering the people, science, and challenges shaping infection prevention with another milestone: its first digital magazine, featuring outbreak analysis, biosecurity, respiratory testing, sterile processing, professional leadership, conference coverage, and more. During National EVS Week, appreciation matters, but partnership matters more. Environmental services professionals bring infection prevention expertise and a unique understanding of the health care environment that can help identify barriers, improve cleaning and disinfection practices, and ultimately protect patients. Nearly 4 months into the DRC's Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak, some indicators suggest transmission may be slowing. But shifting hotspots, treatment-center capacity problems, community deaths, and incomplete surveillance data show why national case totals alone cannot determine whether containment has been achieved. As US measles cases climb into the thousands, immigration has become part of the political debate over the cause. Outbreak data point to a more complex picture involving international travel, declining vaccination coverage, pockets of susceptible populations, and highly efficient measles transmission. CDC reported 3,294 confirmed cases as of September 10. A 10-year NIH-funded study used Bayesian statistical modeling to examine the relationship between continuously active EOScu surfaces and HAI reduction. EOS Surfaces representatives discuss the findings, passive infection prevention, environmental recontamination, and why IPs should continue asking tough questions. CBIC and APIC say updated IPU requirements are intended to protect infection prevention education from commercial influence. But differing guidance, questions about industry support, and concerns about educational access leave IPs asking for a clearer, more consistent road map. Artificial intelligence can help IPs analyze surveillance data, identify patterns, improve training, and reduce repetitive work. Bassel Molaeb explains why AI literacy is becoming an important IPC competency while human validation, clinical context, and professional judgment remain essential. "You can't underinvest in public health and then expect it to have a fast and swift response." Brian C. Castrucci, DrPH, discusses Cyclospora, surveillance, workforce capacity, misinformation, and rebuilding public trust. Read the Q&A and watch the full ICT interview. A surface can look clean and still carry significant bioload. The new Bioload Exposure Metric Index (BEMI) aims to standardize ATP sampling and move surface hygiene toward a measurable cleanliness score. If we can't measure clean, how do we know we've achieved it? Is the Ebola outbreak in the DRC getting better? The answer depends on which numbers you examine. Several important indicators are moving in the right direction, including slower case growth and a declining Rt. But major gaps remain in contact tracing, testing, community deaths, safe burial coverage, and treatment capacity in some of the hardest-hit areas. ICT takes a deeper look at the latest outbreak data and why the numbers suggest cautious optimism, not victory

Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search Support Menu Ebola cases top 9,000 in DR Congo outbreak News brief October 13, 2026 Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Ebola Viral Hemorrhagic Fever Share NIAID The latest numbers from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) show the Ebola outbreak now stands at 9,066 cases 4,381 deaths. This is the second largest Ebola outbreak in history, following the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. The West Africa outbreak was caused by the more common Zaire strain of the virus. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, which has no approved treatments or vaccines. The outbreak’s current case-fatality rate is 48.2%. Phase 2/3 trial starts for Bundibugyo vaccine Today CEPI, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, announced preparations are under way for a phase 2/3 trial called Tumaini, which will evaluate the safety, immunogenicity and efficacy of vaccine candidates against Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), including Ervebo, the Zaire-targeting vaccine. “Tumaini is designed as an adaptive platform trial, subject to ethical and regulatory approval,” CEPI said. “This allows several vaccine candidates to be evaluated in parallel within a single trial framework, which saves valuable time during an outbreak.” In addition to Ervebo, the trial will include at least two Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates. Currently the Bravo study, a research project coordinated by Doctors Without Borders (Medecins sans Frontieres) is evaluating the effectiveness of the Ervebo vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain in North Kivu and Ituri province. Teams have vaccinated 857 frontline workers. Washington state confirms first H5N1 avian flu detection in dairy cattle News brief October 13, 2026 Stephanie Soucheray, MA Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Clara Bastain/iStock Late last week the US Department of Agriculture’s National Veterinary Services Laboratory confirmed the detection of H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) on two Yakima County dairy farms in Washington. “This marks the first known case of HPAI in cattle in Washington state,” state officials said. Since March 2024 dairy cattle herds in 19 states have documented H5N1 infections, including neighboring Idaho. 2 farms under quarantine “Washington State Department of Agriculture conducted on-farm investigations, testing, and gathered additional epidemiological information to better understand this detection and limit further disease spread,” officials said. “The two farms are under quarantine and have employed strict biosecurity measures. Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows.” Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows. In the past 30 days four dairy herds have had H5N1 detections, including herds in Kansas and Texas. So far in 2026, US officials have confirmed avian flu in 93 dairy herds, compared to 917 in 2024 and 171 last year. “We appreciate how difficult this is for our dairy families, farmworkers, and veterinarians that are working hard to keep animals safe and healthy,” said Washington State Veterinarian Amber Itle, VMD. “The most important thing you can do is implement enhanced biosecurity and report symptoms immediately if animals show signs of illness.” Using fake avian flu patients, researchers show need for faster action, better compliance News brief October 13, 2026 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Topics Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Mpox COVID-19 Measles Spotmatik / iStock Unannounced drills to assess healthcare facility readiness to manage infectious disease outbreaks in three areas of the United States revealed variable adherence to containment protocols, according to a new study published in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Using a simulated avian flu scenario involving an A(H5) strain with professional actors as patients, local and national public health authorities conducted 73 drills in 69 emergency departments, urgent care centers, and outpatient clinics in New Jersey, New York, and the US Virgin Islands from January to June 2026. The aim was to assess facilities’ ability to rapidly identify and isolate patients with suspected high-consequence infectious diseases. “Successive recent outbreaks of viral hemorrhagic fevers, novel coronaviruses (e.g., COVID-19), monkeypox [mpox] virus disease, measles, and avian influenza A(H5) have reinforced the importance of rapidly recognizing and safely managing patients with potentially severe transmissible infections at health care facility points of entry, to protect health care workers, patients, and surrounding communities,” the authors wrote. Median time to isolation 1 minute shy of goal Facilities conducted symptom screening in 93.2% of the drills, documented travel history on patient arrival in 79.5%, and asked about exposure to avian flu in 9.6%. In 82.2% of drills during which the patient was appropriately masked, the median time from arrival to masking was two minutes, one minute short of the target. Findings identified opportunities to support these outpatient settings in implementing more robust screening, isolation and notification processes, and IPC training. Of 71.2% of drills that included patient isolation, the median time to isolation was 11 minutes, one minute shy of the 10-minute goal. A combination of masking and isolation took place in 60.3% of exercises. Patient actors were identified as being at risk for avian flu in 63.4% of cases. Infection prevention-and-control (IPC) teams were notified or scheduled to be notified in 54.8% of drills, and staff wore all recommended personal protective equipment (PPE) in just 25.0% but wore none in 5.9%. “These drills identified needs for health care workers and health care facility staff member training to achieve earlier identification, masking, and isolation of potentially infectious febrile patients,” the researchers wrote. “Findings identified opportunities to support these outpatient settings in implementing more robust screening, isolation and notification processes, and IPC training.” In case you missed it Previous Next Kids vaccinated against chickenpox less likely to develop shingles, analysis finds Lawmakers want answers from CDC director on childhood vaccine (Xinhua) KINSHASA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has recorded more than 9,000 confirmed Ebola cases since May, as preparations for a vaccine trial near completion. The country's task force on Ebola released a situation report on Tuesday, showing that 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths had been recorded as of Oct. 11, bringing the overall case fatality rate to 48.3 percent. A total of 2,389 patients have recovered. The outbreak has affected 65 health zones across seven provinces. The eastern province of Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for 73.8 percent of all confirmed cases, followed by North Kivu Province, which has recorded the highest case fatality rate at 57.1 percent. Earlier this month, DRC Health Minister Roger Kamba said that the outbreak was becoming increasingly localized, with several affected health zones reporting no new cases for weeks. However, World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned on Oct. 7 that while the epidemic was slowing in some areas, it continued to grow in others. He also highlighted persistent challenges, including the high proportion of deaths occurring in communities and gaps in contact tracing. The outbreak was caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which no vaccine or treatment has yet been specifically approved, although clinical trials are underway. Ervebo, a vaccine approved against the Zaire ebolavirus, is being administered to frontline health workers under research protocols and through compassionate-use arrangements. According to the latest situation report, 399 frontline workers had been vaccinated in Haut-Uele province as of Oct. 11. Yet its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo ebolavirus remains unproven. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations announced Tuesday that final preparations were underway for Tumaini, a pivotal Phase 2/3 clinical trial to evaluate vaccine candidates against the Bundibugyo virus. The trial, expected to begin in the coming weeks pending ethical and regulatory approval, will likely evaluate Ervebo first, followed by vaccines specifically developed against the strain as they become available. Declared on May 15, the outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest worldwide, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■ Health workers transport an Ebola patient at an Ebola treatment center in Bunia, capital of Ituri Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), on Oct. 12, 2026. (NYSE American:NNVC) (the "Company"), a clinical stage leader developing antiviral drugs that viruses cannot escape, said today that its Phase IIA Ebola Treatment Clinical Trial of NV-387 Oral Gummies is progressing well. The Phase IIA part of the clinical trial is designed to evaluate different dosage regimens of the oral gummies for the treatment of different severity levels of the Ebola Bundibugyo virus infection and disease in the current Ebola Outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo ("DRC"). The trial is enrolling and is expected to continue enrolling persons exhibiting different disease severity levels, in the "Dry Stage" and "Wet Stage". The clinical symptoms of the Ebola BDBV disease are complex, and possibly different from prior Ebola virus outbreaks, as explained in the footnote i. Patients are known to come to the Ebola Treatment Centers only when they feel severely ill. Therefore, we are anticipating mostly "Wet Stage" patients, with severe vomiting and diarrhea, to be the primarily enrolled population. Some patients may not be able to take the oral gummies due to vomiting bouts and may be withdrawn; such subjects would not be considered as evaluable if enrolled. The Phase IIA part of the trial is designed to examine the safety and tolerability of NV-387 oral gummies dosing in the Ebola patients, and the number of days that the drug is tolerated within the context of the disease, starting at 6 days of dosing, and extending by 3 day increments to a maximum of 12 days of treatment. The NV-387 treatment will be stopped when the patient's viral load has become undetectable based on qRT-PCR. Efficacy is not expected to be evaluated in a scientific, statistically significant, manner in such an adaptive treatment scenario. Therefore, and with due ethical consideration, a parallel group of no NV-387 treatment is excluded in this exploratory Phase IIA part. Nevertheless, an efficacy signal can be seen even in this small clinical trial with up to 20 subjects, if NV-387 is highly effective. This can happen if the data of 20 subjects treated with NV-387 is found to be sufficient to statistically discriminate the NV-387 treated group from the general observations of treatment of Ebola patients in the Ebola Treatment Centers in the same area. Ebola Patients in this area have generally experienced an infection-to-fatality rate (IFR) of 67% to 75%. The IFR corrects the data for the fact that the infected person dies on an average about three weeks later, and therefore is a more accurate representation of reality than the crude Case Fatality Rate (CFR) ii. The Company will be able to make an announcement regarding (i) whether NV-387 is found to be sufficiently safe and well tolerated to continue into Phase IIB, and, (ii) if NV-387 group is well discriminated from the general expectation of 67-75% IFR, then whether NV-387 oral gummies treatment demonstrated signs of efficacy against the Ebola Bundibugyo virus; after the Phase IIA clinical trial is completed and a report is prepared by the Principal Investigator's team for formal communication. After an appropriate NV-387 Oral Gummies dosage regimen is identified, it will be used in an expanded, randomized, controlled clinical trial, Part IIB, to evaluate effectiveness of the Oral treatment drug NV-387 Oral Gummies. NV-387 is designed to attack the virus and reduce the viral load in the body. Reducing viral load correlates with improvement in physiological function. Reduction in viral load to undetected level means complete recovery from the viral disease. However, the bodily functions, may take longer time even after reaching undetectable viral load, as the virus-attacked organs rejuvenate. It is also possible that some permanent damage, e.g. kidney damage, may persist even after virological recovery. The current BDBV outbreak has continued to expand, with 9,000 confirmed cases and 4,339 deaths as of October 10, 2026, according to the WHO iii, with all but a few cases in DRC. An Ebola patient was able to travel from DRC via Uganda to Kenya, and died at home there recently, despite travel restrictions. Fortunately after a week, no secondary infections from this patient have been detected (yet). This emphasizes the potential risk to the world, although the possibility of an Ebola outbreak in the USA or globally remains negligible, because of various global travel restrictions. Within DRC, while the initial outbreak sites including Ituri have possibly stabilized, the outbreak has started gaining strength in Nord Kivu province with 40% of national confirmed cases now coming from Nord Kivu, which does not have sufficient ebola treatment centers capacity, with only 29 beds in treatment center, and only about 20 "transit facility" beds for holding suspected cases until diagnosis results come in, according to Doctors Without Borders iv. Recently, thousands of refugees fled from a refugee camp where more than 30 people had died from Ebola BDBV, to escape from security forces that were investigating weapons stored in the camp. Their fleeing has increased the risk of spread v. Additionally, 6 new Ebola cases were recorded in an Eastern part of DRC controlled by rebel groups, further complicating efforts to control the outbreak vi. The USA has been, laudably, and proudly, the largest provider of humanitarian and relief assistance in this outbreak, with almost $1.4 Billion in contributions. The USA has already provided $887 Million, and has pledged another $500 Million, of which $267 million has been released, according to the US Department of State vii. There is no current threat of Ebola in the USA. The US Government is active in ensuring that suspected or confirmed ebolavirus cases do not enter the general population in the USA. To this end, travel from DRC has been restricted, with pre-travel quarantine requirements imposed, and suspect travelers are directed to screening at specific airports and may be further quarantined. Travelers going to and from Central Africa need to constantly check travel restrictions as well as travel limitations in light of these changing outbreak conditions. It is apparent that travel restrictions have been able to control the outbreak periphery to DRC alone (with few early cases in Uganda) minimizing risk to the rest of the world. There is no approved Treatment or Vaccine for the new variant of the Bundibugyo Ebolavirus (BDBV) that is causing the current rapidly expanding outbreak of the Ebolavirus Disease (EVD) in DRC. The rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola virus causing the current outbreak appears to be its new variant, likely freshly introduced from some animal source viii, such as fruit bats. NV-387 is a broad-spectrum antiviral that mimics the host-side features that the virus requires, and is likely to be effective against Ebola viruses because they use the same host-side feature mimicked by NV-387. NV-387 Oral Gummies is a drug product readily delivered orally. It does not even require swallowing effort or water, because it dissolves in the mouth by itself, simplifying delivery for even sick individuals with swallowing difficulties. This oral delivery is an important feature that puts NV-387, a broad-spectrum antiviral, as being superior to the other approaches. "Only safe and effective broad-spectrum antiviral drugs like NV-387 that can effectively tackle most viral infections will enable the world to combat viruses and defend the global population in the war against known and unknown nanoscopic enemies that are viruses," commented Dr. Diwan, adding, "Today, NV-387 is the only drug in clinical development with such broad-spectrum potential that promises to combat diverse epidemics like Mpox and Ebola, and even Measles, to the best of our knowledge." The outbreak which was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern ("PHEIC") by the WHO on May 17, 2026, continues to rapidly expand, outpacing containment efforts. The outbreak arose in a high traffic region bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with travel contacts to Uganda, and South Sudan and with 11 more nations in Africa at risk ix. NV-387 is a broad-spectrum antiviral that mimics the host-side feature called heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG) that over 90-95% of human pathogenic viruses require for infecting cells. No matter how much the virus changes in the field, it continues to use HSPG, and therefore it cannot escape the drug NV-387. In contrast, Remdesivir is a small molecule inhibitor of the viral RDRP enzyme needed for making copies of the viral genome, and the virus can possibly escape by small number of mutations. All Ebola viruses utilize HSPG as the attachment receptor prior to gaining entry into the cell. Thereafter, followed by entry into the cell inside endosomes, the ebolavirus surface glycoprotein is substantially degraded, opening up its site for binding to its cognate receptor called NPC1, thereby entering into the cytoplasm where the next steps in its replication begin. Thus there is a strong rationale that NV-387 could be highly effective against Ebola virus infections, not just Bundibugyo, but also the Sudan and other viruses for which there are no treatments. All previous anti-Ebola efforts have been focused on vaccines and antibodies x. This has led to approval of therapies that are specific to the Ebolavirus Zaire strain only, albeit with limited effectiveness. This leaves out all other filoviruses of consequence: Sudan, Marburg, and the more rare Bundibugyo with no treatment or vaccine. In contrast, if NV-387, as a broad-spectrum antiviral, is found to be effective against the Bundibugyo virus, it will likely be effective against all ebolaviruses and possibly all filoviruses; that would be a game changer for pandemic preparedness. At present, BDBV has been consistently demonstrating high crude CFR of 48% and IFR of 67% in DRC. Therefore, BDBV is of great concern as a potential pandemic disease. However, it is believed that ebolaviruses do not transmit via respiratory droplets or aerosols and rather require extensive contact with bodily fluids of an infected person. In addition, within DRC and internationally, certain protective quarantine measures for travel from the outbreak areas have been implemented. Therefore, currently there is no apparent threat of a global pandemic. With ever-increasing global travel, local outbreaks such as ebola can quickly travel far and wide potentially causing global pandemics, as was the case with COVID-19, if not caught in time. It is not feasible to produce a new vaccine and a new set of antibody drugs to combat every possible virus. Renew subscription Maybe later Subscribe for a month to get full access What top Kenyan expert says you need to know about deadly virus Friday, October 09, 2026 The confirmation of Kenya’s first Ebola case should end the comfortable fiction that preparedness is measured by the number of people screened at airports. Photo credit: Shutterstock By Hellen Shikanda Health and Science Reporter Nation Media Group What you need to know: Ebola disease is a serious infectious illness caused by viruses in the Orthoebolavirus genus, within the filovirus family. It begins with fever, headache and muscle pain. It can quickly progress to vomiting and diarrhoea and damage the liver and kidneys. Kenya had never recorded a confirmed Ebola case since 1976, when it was first recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The disease has caused repeated outbreaks worldwide. That streak was broken this week when a 39-year-old Kenyan man from the DRC was found to have Ebola. We speak with Professor Marianne Mureithi, Medical Microbiology and Immunology professor and KAVI-ICR director at the University of Nairobi. Prof Marianne Mureithi, 45, the first female medical microbiology professor at the University of Nairobi. Photo credit: Pool What is Ebola Disease? Ebola disease is a serious infectious illness caused by viruses in the Orthoebolavirus genus, within the filovirus family. These include Zaire, Sudan and Bundibugyo viruses. How does it manifest? It begins with fever, headache and muscle pain. The disease can quickly progress to vomiting and diarrhoea and, in severe cases, damage the liver and kidneys. Some patients develop bleeding. How does it spread from one person to another? You have to be in close contact with someone who has Ebola. It does not spread through the air like Covid-19. Transmission occurs through direct contact with an infected person who is ill. People who develop symptoms should disclose their travel history. Early recognition and prompt treatment can improve survival. Why do we call the different types of Ebola viruses, and not variants like we did with Covid-19? Ebola is a broader group of diseases. With Covid-19, Delta and Omicron are variants of SARS-CoV-2. With Ebola, they are distinct species within the same genus. The larger family is called Orthoebolavirus, with species distinct enough to be classified separately, and each can have variants. This matters because a vaccine or treatment that works against one may not work against another. Since the three viruses are not mutations, where then did the Bundibugyo virus come from? It may have originated elsewhere, but it was first identified in Uganda. Ebola viruses are zoonotic, and fruit bats are among the suspected natural reservoirs, although the precise reservoir and source of individual spillover events are not always established. Bundibugyo virus was first identified during an outbreak in Uganda in 2007, with subsequent outbreaks reported, including in the DRC. Is it easy to establish the first ever person that was infected? The first infected person cannot be established. Scientists can use next-generation sequencing to identify and characterise the virus. For Bundibugyo, this was done by the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Is Bundibugyo more infectious than Zaire and Sudan? Available evidence does not show that Bundibugyo virus is inherently more transmissible than other Ebola viruses. Mortality has varied between viruses and outbreaks. Historical Bundibugyo outbreaks have often reported lower deaths than many Ebola outbreaks. The observed case-fatality ratio is influenced by detection, speed of care and quality of treatment. A high death toll alone does not prove increased lethality. What concern do you have with the Bundibugyo virus now? The concern with Bundibugyo is the lack of proven medical tools. There is no licensed vaccine or approved treatment specifically for this virus. Rapid detection, good clinical care and prevention of transmission are therefore important. Now that there’s no specific treatment for Bundibugyo, how then are they managing the disease? Early and intensive supportive care improves survival. Clinicians manage fever, replace fluids and electrolytes, and monitor kidney injury, electrolyte disturbances and low blood pressure. Patients need a designated treatment facility and protected staff. Why is the incubation period for this disease indicated as 21 days? The incubation period for Ebola disease is generally two to 21 days. This range is based on observed exposure histories. The 21-day upper limit is why contacts are followed for 21 days. People are not considered infectious before symptoms begin; transmission occurs through infected body fluids or contaminated materials. Where are we in terms of vaccine development? There is no licensed Bundibugyo-specific vaccine. Candidate vaccines, including platforms from Oxford and IAVI, are under development. These are candidate vaccines in clinical development. What happens at different levels of the clinical trials? Phase 1 assesses safety, dose and immune response. Phase 2 involves more participants and refines the vaccination schedule. Phase 3 assesses protection against disease. Phase 4 involves continued monitoring after approval and wider use. Has Kenya ever been part of previous vaccine trials? KAVI-ICR, University of Nairobi, contributed to the global Ebola vaccine programme. KAVI-ICR conducted a Nairobi Phase 1 trial of Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo and later participated in Phase 2 evaluation. The Nairobi Phase 1 study generated African safety and immunogenicity data published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. The work reflects KAVI-ICR’s capacity to conduct vaccine trials and contribute African evidence. The licensed Zaire Ebola vaccine, Ervebo, is now being evaluated in the current Bundibugyo outbreak under research protocols. Its protection against Bundibugyo remains unknown, although animal data suggest possible cross-protection. How many times should people be tested before they’re declared negative? It depends on whether the person is suspected or recovering from confirmed Ebola. For suspected cases, specimen timing matters. A negative molecular test very early in illness may not exclude infection, so repeat testing is guided by symptom timing, clinical suspicion and the applicable national testing algorithm. For a confirmed patient recovering from Ebola, protocols commonly require clinical recovery and two consecutive negative blood tests, ideally at least 48 hours apart. The treatment team follows the national discharge protocol. How exactly is an Ebola test done? Once you present yourself, there needs to be a laboratory that can confirm the infection. In the lab, a trained person safely collects blood using Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), and reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) detects genetic material from the virus. Testing uses validated assays in designated laboratories with strict biosafety and infection-control procedures. The test must be capable of detecting Bundibugyo virus. If an early sample is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, repeat testing is guided by symptom timing and the applicable national testing algorithm. Confirmation and referral follow the national testing algorithm. Reference laboratories can use genomic sequencing to characterise the virus and support outbreak investigations. hshikanda@ke.nationmedia.com Follow our WhatsApp channel for breaking news updates and more stories like this. Three viruses are known to have caused large Ebola disease outbreaks: Ebola virus, Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus. Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;) Ebola: 10 Things to Know About Highly Contagious Illness as Kenya Confirms First Case Source: Getty Images The disease got its name from the Ebola River, located near Yambuku, in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). With Kenya recently confirming its first case, TUKO.co.ke shares 10 key facts about the highly contagious illness. 1. How deadly is Ebola? Ebola disease has an average case fatality rate of around 50%, although the fatality rate has varied significantly between outbreaks, ranging from approximately 25% to 90%. PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger. The World Health Organisation (WHO) reports that early and intensive supportive care can improve a patient's chances of survival. Treatment can include rehydration, management of symptoms, nutritional support and treatment of other infections or complications. 2. How does Ebola spread? Ebola is believed to have natural hosts among fruit bats. The virus enters the human population when people come into close contact with infected animals or those that have died from the disease. Read also US govt issues statement after Kenya's first Ebola patient dies These may include fruit bats, chimpanzees, gorillas, monkeys, forest antelopes and porcupines. Once the virus is circulating among humans, it can spread through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. People can also become infected by touching objects or surfaces contaminated with bodily fluids such as blood, faeces or vomit. 3. Can Ebola spread before symptoms appear? WHO adds that people do not transmit Ebola before they develop symptoms. However, they remain infectious for as long as the virus is present in their blood. This makes infection prevention and control measures particularly important when caring for someone who has developed symptoms. 4. Why are healthcare workers at risk? Healthcare and care workers have frequently become infected during Ebola outbreaks. This can happen when they have close contact with infected patients and appropriate infection prevention and control measures are not strictly followed. Special precautions are therefore required when treating suspected or confirmed Ebola patients. Apart from healthcare environments, traditional burial ceremonies can contribute to transmission if mourners have direct contact with the body of someone who died from Ebola. Read also WHO issues statement on lockdown after Kenya's first Ebola patient dies in Nairobi Safe and dignified burials are therefore an important part of controlling an outbreak. 5. What are the symptoms of Ebola? The incubation period, the time between infection and the appearance of symptoms, can range from two to 21 days. Symptoms can begin suddenly and may include fever, fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, headache, a sore throat, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rashes, and impaired kidney or liver function. Some patients can also experience confusion, irritability and aggression as the disease affects the central nervous system. 6. Does Ebola always cause bleeding? No. Although Ebola is often associated with severe bleeding, this is less common and may occur later in the illness. Some patients can develop internal or external bleeding, including blood in vomit or faeces, nosebleeds, bleeding from the gums, and bleeding from sites where needles have punctured the skin. 7. Why is Ebola difficult to diagnose? The early symptoms of Ebola can resemble those of several other diseases. These include malaria, typhoid fever, shigellosis, meningitis and other viral haemorrhagic fevers. Read also Kenya's first Ebola patient: A timeline of movements from DRC to Nairobi Laboratory testing is therefore required to confirm an infection. Diagnostic methods include RT-PCR, antibody-capture ELISA, antigen-capture detection tests and virus isolation through cell culture. Because patient samples can pose an extreme biohazard risk, they require specialised handling and laboratory testing procedures. 8. Is there treatment for Ebola? There is no single treatment that applies to all Ebola diseases. However, early intensive supportive care can improve survival. Supportive care can include rehydration, pain management, nutritional support, appropriate testing and treatment of complications and co-infections such as malaria. For Ebola virus disease, WHO recommends two monoclonal antibody treatments: Ansuvimab (mAb114) and REGN-EB3 (Inmazeb). There are currently no approved specific therapeutics for Sudan virus disease or Bundibugyo virus disease, although candidate treatments are being developed and studied. 9. Is there an Ebola vaccine? There are two vaccines listed by WHO for Ebola virus disease: Ervebo and Zabdeno and Mvabea. Ervebo is recommended as part of outbreak response and can be accessed through the International Coordinating Group on vaccine provision when there is a confirmed Ebola virus disease outbreak. Read also Ivorian socialite Fatim Bakayoko reportedly dies after undergoing BBL surgery in Nigeria However, vaccines and specific treatments are not yet approved for all Ebola viruses. 10. How can Ebola outbreaks be controlled? Containing an Ebola outbreak requires several measures working together. These include early diagnosis and intensive supportive care, infection prevention and control, and disease surveillance. Contact tracing, laboratory testing, holding safe and dignified burials, vaccinations, as well as community and social mobilisation can also help prevent outbreaks. Early detection and treatment are particularly important because seeking medical care promptly can improve a patient's chances of survival. Timeline of Kenya's First Ebola Patient Kenya's first confirmed Ebola patient travelled from the DRC through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on October 3. Health CS Aden Duale confirmed the case on October 6, with at least 28 contacts already identified for monitoring. Authorities are tracing 23 passengers who shared a flight with the patient as contact tracing efforts intensify. The Health Ministry reported 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths, with the death toll approaching half the number of confirmed cases. The rising death toll has alarmed health workers and authorities, with a large share of recorded deaths occurring outside treatment centers. The latest report recorded 88 new cases and warned that “community transmission remains a concern." The outbreak has created new hot spots as it spreads to more communities, with 65 health zones across seven provinces now affected. Officials say the confirmed cases account for only a third of all cases, with many going undetected. The outbreak involves the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Efforts to contain the virus have been impaired by several factors, including fighting between government forces and rebel groups, which has created one of the world's direst humanitarian crises, widespread disregard for health precautions, intense population movements and shortages of medical supplies and treatment centers. The outbreak has surpassed Congo's 16 previous outbreaks in scale and is on track to top the 2014-2016 West Africa regional outbreak that killed 11,000 people. Phase Ib trials of the ChAdOx1 vaccine, developed by the University of Oxford, began in Uganda on Oct. 6, Wessam Mankoula told a virtual news conference. Mankoula, lead of the continental incident management support team for the Ebola response, said Phase Ia trials began in Britain in July. He said another candidate vaccine developed by Moderna recently received ethical approval for Phase Ib trials in Uganda after its Phase Ia trials began in Canada in August. Congo has recorded 8,728 confirmed Ebola cases, including 4,205 deaths, since the outbreak was declared in May, according to the latest Health Ministry update. The latest epidemic has affected seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and South-Ubangi. Kenya reported its first imported case this week involving a patient who died after traveling from Congo. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, for which no vaccine or treatment has been approved. In August, Congo was allocated 70,000 Ervebo vaccines from the global Ebola virus disease vaccine stockpile for use in the current outbreak. The vaccine is approved for use against the Zaire Ebola virus. More than 7,700 healthcare and other frontline workers have so far been vaccinated, Mankoula said. The findings of the assessment will guide the Organization’s activities with media outlets to improve access to reliable information adapted to local realities and address false information more effectively. They will also support the work of health authorities and humanitarian agencies on the ground. This initiative forms part of UNESCO’s contribution to the Ebola response by strengthening access to reliable information, building community trust, and helping people adopt appropriate preventive measures. Since 15 May 2026, Ituri Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has been facing a new Ebola outbreak. Caused by the Bundibugyo virus, it is the 17th Ebola outbreak recorded in the country. Early detection of cases, timely access to care and the implementation of public health measures all help contain its spread. However, the response also depends on the quality of the information available to communities and their trust in response actors. Information that is difficult to understand or distorted by disinformation can fuel mistrust and delay access to care. Against this backdrop, UNESCO conducted a rapid assessment in Bunia to better understand people’s information and media habits and needs. Engaging communities With technical support from the Ituri Collective of Community and Local Radio Stations (CORACOPI) and the Federation of Community Radio Stations of the Congo, interviews have been conducted with 30 adults of different ages, including 14 women. The survey explored the sources they consulted, the level of trust placed in those sources and the rumours to which they had been exposed. Although conducted with a limited sample, the assessment identifies several trends and provides concrete insights to inform future media-related activities. The assessment followed a workshop organized by UNESCO in Bunia on 8 and 9 July 2026, in collaboration with the DRC Ministry of Communication and Media and the Federation of Community Radio Stations of Congo. The training strengthened the capacities of 40 journalists, including 17 women, in health risk communication, fact-checking, ethical reporting and addressing mis/disinformation. UNESCO Radio as the leading source of information Among those interviewed, radio emerged as the main source of information about Ebola. Most participants listen to it daily, and it also enjoys a high level of trust. Its close connection with communities makes it an effective channel for sharing verified information about the outbreak. Health workers are another key source, particularly for explaining symptoms, treatments and vaccination. International organizations, public authorities and, to a lesser extent, community and religious leaders are also trusted by participants. Social media, particularly WhatsApp and Facebook, complements these sources, especially among young adults. However, these platforms are also among the spaces where misinformation and disinformation circulate, alongside rumours shared within neighbourhoods and certain traditional or religious beliefs. Within this sample, women respondents reported combining several sources of information more frequently, including radio, word of mouth and social media. These practices highlight the value of sharing verified information through both local radio stations and the digital platforms used by residents, while also equipping people to identify reliable sources and verify content before sharing it. Practical questions about the disease and how to stay safe The information needs expressed by participants relate directly to the decisions people must make when faced with the disease. They particularly want to know how to recognize symptoms, understand modes of transmission and preventive measures, and respond when a family member shows signs of Ebola. Language is another important aspect of accessibility. Although French remains the most frequently requested language, survey participants, particularly women, also expressed a preference for information in Swahili and Lingala. Providing content in these languages would better reflect local language use and help reduce misunderstandings. Participants also favoured several formats for receiving information, including interactive radio programmes, SMS messages, community awareness sessions and illustrated materials. Combining these channels could help reach different audiences, including people whose access to the internet is restricted by power cuts or the cost of mobile data. The impact of disinformation on behaviours The rumours identified through the assessment concern some of the very issues that generate the most questions. They include claims that response teams are deliberately spreading the virus or that certain injections transmit Ebola. Some participants said they initially believed these claims but later changed their minds after receiving information from radio stations or health workers. These accounts suggest that mis- and disinformation often gains ground when clear explanations are lacking. When questions remain unanswered, rumours can fill the gap, but their influence may recede when credible sources provide reliable information. The challenge is therefore not only to refute rumours, but also to communicate early, clearly explain response procedures, particularly vaccination, and give residents opportunities to put their questions directly to knowledgeable professionals. Findings to guide the next phase of the response The assessment points towards an approach grounded in the practices observed in Bunia. Radio is the most widely used source and enjoys a high level of trust, while health workers provide the expertise people seek about the disease. Both have also helped several participants reconsider rumours they initially believed. Local languages and a range of communication formats can make this information accessible to a broader audience. The findings will guide the next activities. One priority is to build sustained links between community radio stations and health workers, including through interactive programmes in which listeners can ask questions directly. Another is to address the information gaps identified by communities, which can create fertile ground for rumours. Finally, the assessment confirms the need to strengthen the capacities of media outlets, particularly community media, in risk communication and fact-checking, enabling them to contribute to community resilience during the current outbreak and future health emergencies.
